War department
July 1, 1794

Sir,

Some doubts having arisen in several of the States as to the circumstances of equipment in any vessel belonging to the belligerent Nations which may be deemed an unlawful encrease or augmentation of force, it has been judged adviseable in order that an uniform principle may prevail upon the subject to give the following explanation.

The mounting additional Guns, or changing or altering the calibre or the size of the Guns in any manner whatever, the making of new Gun barriages or the cutting of new Port Holes in any part of a vessel are each adjudged to be an unlawful augmentation of force and therefore to be prevented.

This construction had its full operation upon the British letter of Marque Ship Juno, which arrived in the port of Philadelphia in the Month of July 1793. New Gun barriages were made, additional Guns mounted which had been brought in the hold of the said vessel and new port Holes were cut in her sides and stern. Each and every one of these Acts being deemed unlawful she was obliged to reland the new Gun barriages, dismount the additional Guns and dismantle and effectually close up the new port Holes —

Although this Rule has been hitherto considered as applicable to the belligerent powers only; yet in order to prevent any abuse or national responsibility from the subjects of other neutral nations fitting out or equipping vessels in our ports for the use of one of the warring nations it is extended to all vessels belonging even to Neutrals.

The United States being also a neutral Nation, the vessels of their citizens in most cases do not require to be armed. the arming of such vessels therefore raises a presumption that it is done with an hostile intent and contrary to the prohibitions of the Act of Congress. Some special cases indeed may occur in which arming may be proper and necessary, but these cases ought always to be well examined and ascertained, lest they should [undecipherable: probable reading: connexions] with some of the belligerent powers. To guard against such an abuse no vessel belonging to any Citizen of the United States is to be permitted to be armed and to sail until after all circumstances concerning her shall have been transmitted to the President and his decision thereon made known.

I have the honor to transmit herein enclosed a new Rule <sup>of War</sup> to the sailing of vessels of belligerent Nations from the United States and also an Act entitled "An Act in addition to an Act for the punishment of certain Crimes against the United States."

I have the honor to be
with great Respect
Your Excellency's
obedient Servant

H Knox

I am with great esteem
Sir

[N° 80. To Major Gen'l Knox Secretary from —]

Head Quarters
Greeneville 7. July 1794.

Sir,

At 7 o'Clock in the morning of the 30 ultimo, one of our escorts consisting of ninety riflemen & fifty Dragoons commanded by Major McMahon was attacked by a very numerous body of Indians under the walls of Fort Recovery followed by a general assault upon that Port & Garrison in every direction.—

The Enemy were soon repulsed with great slaughter, but immediately rallied and reiterated the attack keeping up a very heavy and constant fire at a more respectable distance all that day, which was answered with spirit & effect by the Garrison & that part of Major McMahon's command that had regained the Port.—

The Savages were employed during the night which was dark & foggy in carrying off their dead by torch light which occasionally drew a fire from the Garrison; they nevertheless succeeded so well that there were but eight dead bodies left upon the field & three close under the influence of the fire from the Fort.

The enemy again renewed the attack in the morning of the 1 instant but were ultimately compelled to retreat about one o'clock of that day with loss & disgrace from that very field where they had upon a former occasion been proudly victorious.—

Enclosed is a particular & general return of the killed, wounded & missing — among the killed we have to lament the loss of four good & gallant officers viz. Major McMahon, Capt. Hartshorne, Lieut Craig of the rifle corps & Cornet Torrey of the Cavalry, who all fell in the first charges; among the wounded are the intrepid Capt. Taylor of the Dragoons and Lieut Drake of the Infantry.—

It would appear that the real object of the enemy was to have carried that Port by a coup de main, for they could not possibly have received intelligence of the escort under Major McMahon which only marched from this place on the morning of the 29 ultimo & deposited the supplies the same morning at Fort Recovery, from whence the escort was to have returned at reveille the next morning; therefore then being found at that Post was an accidental &, perhaps, unfortunate moment — by every information as well as from the extent of their movements, which were perfectly square & regular and the line of march in Seventeen columns forming a wide & extended front, their numbers could not have been less than from 1500 to 2000 warriors — it would appear also that they were rather short of provision as they killed & ate a number of pack horses in their encampment the evening after the assault & also at their next encampment on their retreat which was but seven miles from Fort Recovery where they remained two nights, probably from being much encumbered with their dead and wounded — a considerable number of the Pack horses were actually loaded with the dead.—

Permit me now Sir, to express my highest approbation of the bravery & undauntedness of every officer & soldier of the Garrison & escort upon this trying occasion; and as it would be difficult to discriminate between officers equally meritorious & emulous for glory I have directed the Adjutant General to annex the names of every officer of the garrison & escort who were fortunate enough to escape uninjured, being equally exposed to danger with those who are less fortunate.

But I should be wanting in my gratitude were I to omit mentioning in particular Capt. Alex. Gibson of the 4<sup>th</sup> Sub Legion the Commandant & gallant defender of Fort Recovery.—

Sir

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your Excellency's answer to my letter of the 13<sup>th</sup> instant; communicated in a letter from the Secretary at War, dated yesterday; and it is with peculiar regret that I perceive the embarrassment of my situation, relatively to the Requisition establishment, encreasing with every addition to the correspondence which the subject has produced. I certainly Sir have hitherto proceeded upon the presumption, that, whatever form of words may have been employed, it was your request, that the execution of the Requisition law should, for the present, be suspended; and as you possessed all the information, upon which that request was founded, I have thought, likewise, that you would readily assume the responsibility attached to a prompt and confidential compliance with it. But when the Secretary at War remarks that you never contemplated carrying your opinions upon the subject further than to state them as strongly as they were conceived; he leaves it to be inferred, that, for all the consequences of the suspension, without possessing the information, or perhaps on retaining the sentiments only, that led to the measure, I am deemed to be exclusively responsible. This idea claims and justifies, on my part, the almost circum-spection: and I am persuaded, that, while the Executive of the general government, is solicitous to avoid reproach for inattention, or a neglect to make full representations of any danger which is apprehended to the interests of the Union; a similar solicitude in the Executive of a particular government, to avoid reproach either for transgressing the Constitutional bounds of his authority, or for sacrificing the Interests of the State, will be equally approved and indulged.

Hence, Sir I have been induced, in order satisfactorily to compare your opinions on this occasion, with my constitutional and legal powers, to take the advice of the Attorney General of Pennsylvania; and I have the honor to inclose a Copy of the letter in which his sentiments are expressed.

From this document you will perceive, that, although any delay, consistent with the performance of the duties enjoined upon me, may be permitted, a delay which will prevent the execution of the law within the time prescribed will not be justifiable. It is of importance, therefore, to know how long the temporary obstacles, which induced you to advise the suspension of the establishment at [undecipherable: probable "Presque Isle"], are expected to continue; for, if they should not be shortly removed, I must either direct the Commissioners to proceed in laying out the Town, or in resorting to the alternative suggested by the Attorney General, convene the Legislature upon the occasion. The latter measure, however, I shall not think it expedient to adopt, unless you explicitly request it.

Sir,

I have Received your Letter of the 7<sup>th</sup> Instant with its Enclosures —

The boat for the Revenue Office at Wheeling was furnished immediately on Receipt of your Order —

I believe the Whiskey has been Received at this Post and forwarded, agreable to the Secretary of the Treasury's Instructions [strikethrough: a Statement of that] that buisness will appear in the Quarterly Return by next Post

The Inclosed Requisition of Medicines is made by Doctor M'Crea, for the Garrison of Fort Franklin —

About day break in the morning of the 15 Instant a Number of Armed Men Attacked General Neville's House, he himself only defending it, he however dispersed the party having wounded five or Seven, One of whom it is said Mortally — And Yesterday a large Number of Armed Men amounting it is said to Seven hundred Assembled & Attacked his house, defended only by himself Major Kirkpatrick and ten Soldiers, during the attack General Neville finding it impossible to defend the House against Such Numbers, took an Opportunity of escaping and Concealing himself in a Thicket, Major Kirkpatrick continued to defended the House, till One of his men was Killed and four Wounded — having killed two and Wounded Several of the Insurgents, as soon as the Major furnished the Enemy got fire to the House, which is consumed to ashes, it all the Property it Contained, not a Single Article Saved, only the Clothing the Family had, when escaped during the attack, previous to burning the House they had Set fire to the Barn Stable, Kitchen & Granary, which were also Consumed with their Contents, amongst which were Several Valuable Horses and a large Quantity of Grain —

Major Senor Cole Neville, Myself & two others in Attempting to get into the House with a Supply of Ammunition, were made Prisoners, dis-armed & Confined, till the Action was Over, and then Carried Several Miles to their Rendezvous, treating Major Lenox with the Utmost Indignity, and all of Us with Insult all the night, I was happy enough to make my escape, and to find General Neville & to Escort him to my House, were he now is, — I have not yet Slept from my Return and feel very Unwell —

I am Sir,
your Most Obedt.
Hum<sup>le</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>,
I. Craig

War Department
July 28. 1794.

Sir

your Excellency's letter of the 18 instant to the President of the United States has been duly received. It certainly was not his intention that any personal embarrassment should be produced to you from the suppression of the establishment at Presqu'isle. It has been uniformly presented to your Excellency to be tried with that it should be suspended until efforts should be made for removing the temporary obstacles. The expression of this wish was a duty; in as much, as an harmonious cooperation of the State Government with the general Government must always be necessary upon subjects in which the movements of the former may effectually counteract those of the latter. Still the President does not mean to press upon your Excellency the slightest infringement of your constitutional or legal powers, for while he himself pursues the constitution and laws of the United States he shall always observe respect to those of individual States. Whatsoever responsibility therefore is attached to the communication of his desire to your Excellency, he readily assumes and he deems it a fortunate circumstance that you have thought yourself hitherto at liberty to comply with it.

How long the temporary obstacles to this settlement will continue it is impossible to determine. They will certainly last until the campaign against the Western Indians is ended and the disposition of the Six Nations should be materially changed. Neither your Excellency nor the Attorney General have defined the period to which the suspension under the circumstances, stated by him be legally continued. But as the enlistments of the Troops do not expire before the first of December and may be continued longer and as the period for allowing bounties for actual settlement does not close before the first of May, it is evident, that there is sufficient time for holding a treaty with the Six Nations, if begun about the middle of September. A Commissioner will attend for that purpose in behalf of the United States at Canandarqua on the fifteenth day of September next, and their chiefs will be invited thither: as the object will be not only to prevent them from engaging in hostility against us, but also to produce an acquiesence in the settlement proposed; it may be naturally expected that the objections to the purchase will stand very forward. It might prove beneficial if a Commissioner could be sent from Pennsylvania. But it appears from your Excellency's last letter that this cannot be done our Commissioner therefore will take charge of the

documents, which you have promised and will use his best endeavours to quiet the discontents. He will not be authorized to make any concessions injurious to the Title nor to give expectation of any further compensation from your State. If he cannot accommodate the dispute under the influence of the United States by proper explanations he will report the result as the basis of ulterior measures.

I have the honor to be
with great respect
Your Excellency's
obedient Servant
Henry Knox
Secretary of War.

His Excellency

Governor Mifflin

Sir,

I have receiv'd a letter from the Secretary of War, dated the 21<sup>st</sup> instant, in which he informs me of your intention to appoint a Commissioner, for the purpose of holding a Treaty with the Six Nations at Canandaigua, on the 15<sup>th</sup> of September next; and I shall with all possible dispatch transmit, for your information, the documents relating to the title of Pennsylvania, so far as it is founded on a Purchase of the Indian Claims, within the limits particularly designated in the late Council at Le Boeuf. — But at the same time, I [undecipherable] it to be clearly understood that on my part, no assent is given to any proposition that shall bring into doubt, or Controvert, the Rights of the State.—

With Respect to the opinion expressed by the Secretary of War, that (before the lapse of the [undecipherable] during which [undecipherable: probable reading "the Pioneer's"] Settlement may lawfully be Suspended,) there is a sufficient time for holding a Treaty with the Six Nations, if begun about the middle of September, I confess my Judgement has not dictated the same [strikethrough: Conclusion] from a consideration of the Circumstances, which the Case presents to my View. It is true, as the Secretary of War observes, that the enlistments of the Troops do not expire till the first of December, & that they may be continued until the meeting of the Legislature,

that is until the 2<sup>d</sup> of December: but, independent of the Various Casualties, which usually protract and sometimes defeat the project of Indian Treaties, it must be obvious, that a knowledge of the result of a Treaty, held at Canandaigua on the 15<sup>th</sup> of September, cannot reasonably be expected in the City, till the middle of October; that after knowing the result, a fortnight, or three Weeks must necessarily be employed in notifying the Commissioners, and in the prosecution of their Journey to Presque isle; and that by a progress of this kind, the Surveys must be executed (if any man, indeed, can then be found so hardy as to undertake the task) in the depth of Winter, and at the very moment, when the Authority for affording protection to the Commissioners, expires by its own limitation.—

Nor is the Subject without embarrassment, when we consider it, in Relation to the [undecipherable] persons to the persons who shall actually inhabit and reside in the Town on or before the first of May 1795; for no residence can take place till the Surveys are returned; and the Surveys cannot be returned under the Circumstances which have been remarked, till the Winter, and its effects have probably rendered it impracticable to travel to the Settlement within the limited period. — Not only may public policy be thus defeated; but the hopes of many adventurous individuals will be totally destroyed.—

Under the impression of these Considerations, I might be tempted to express a wish that an earlier day should be fixed, for holding the proposed Treaty; but that a sense of duty Suggests an impropriety in the Slightest interference upon the occasion — I will content myself, therefore, with informing you that I shall instruct the Commissioners to hold themselves in readiness to perform their trust, as soon as the Treaty is over: — if the Issue is favourable to our object, they will be authorised, immediately to proceed to Presque isle; but if the Indians shall continue to threaten oppression, directions will be given to wait for a further Communication from me. — In the latter event, I shall rely upon receiving the Military Aid of the General Government, not only to prevent any uneasiness that may arise from the expiration of the Pennsylvania Enlistments, but effectually to subdue that Resistance to the Execution of this Law of Pennsylvania; which its Suspension, by giving time and Confidence to our Ill-disposed Neighbours, must naturally increase.—

I am, with perfect Respect,
Your Excellency's
most Obed<sup>t</sup> Hble Svt
Thomas Mifflin

War department
August 7. 1794

Sir,

The President of the United States after the most solemn deliberation has deemed it vincumbent upon him to issue the proclamation herein enclosed and to take other measures for causing the laws of the United States to be duly observed in the Western parts of the State of Pennsylvania according to the purport of the said proclamation.

In pursuance of this determination he has directed me to request your Excellency forthwith to issue your orders for organizing and holding in readiness to march at a moments warning a troop of the Militia of Virginia amounting to Three thousand three hundred non commissioned Officers and privates — with a due proportion of commissioned Officers according to my letter of the 19 May last armed and equipped as completely as possible with the articles in possession of the State of Virginia or of the Individuals who shall compose the troops.

If however it should be impracticable to arm and equip completely the said Corps, the deficiency will be furnished by the United States on information thereof being transmitted to this Office, as will also Tents, Camp Kettles, and other articles of Camp Equipage and Musket Cartridges, Artillery and the Ammunition and Apparatus thereunto belonging.

It is desired that the Corps should consist of Three thousand Infantry and three thousand Cavalry. This is mentioned as a general idea, but your Excellency will regulate its composition according to the facility with which troops of different descriptions may be obtained.

As soon as this Corps shall be in readiness your Excellency will please to notify the same to this Office. The times and places of rendezvous will be hereafter designated. The President defers naming them at present and until the effect of certain pacific measures which he is about trying with the deluded insurgents shall be known.

An arrangement for furnishing Rations and other necessary supplies will be hereafter notified.

The forces to be called out will be according to the following schedule —

Maryland — — 2000 . . 200 . . . 150.
Virginia — — 3000 — 300 — —

I have the honor to be
with great Respect

obedient Servant

Sir,

The Secretary at War being absent from the Seat of Government I am directed by the President to write to you on the subject of those French privateers, fitted out in [strikethrough: our ports,] which you have heretofore been informed, were to be denied Asylum within the United States, except upon the condition of being dismantled of their military equipments.

The subsequent conduct of some of these Vessels is a matter of real embarrasment and disatisfaction. By running from one port to another they have in effect enjoyed the asylum which it was intended to deny them, and have thereby placed the Government in the unpleasant situation not only of seeing itself trifled with, but of being liable to the suspicion of connivance in an evasion of its positive assurances to Foreign Powers.

It is inadmissible that such a state of things should continue, and therefore the President has come to a resolution to cause every such Vessel, which since the promulgation of his instructions to refuse them asylum shall have been in a port of the United States [strikethrough: or not] [strikethrough: has had] an opportunity to acquire a knowledge of that instruction, and which shall hereafter be found in any port or district of the United States, to be deprived of her military equipments.

I have it in instruction from him to communicate this resolution to you, and to request your effectual cooperation in carrying it into execution within the State of [underline: Connecticut].

While the reasons which have been assigned, beget a solicitude in the President that the measure may be punctually and completely executed, there are weighty considerations which induce him to wish that it may be found practicable to accomplish it in each case without bloodshed. To this end, it will be useful that any force which may be employed for this purpose should be such as will controul a disposition to resist.

with perfect respect

I have the honor to be
Sir

47815:
York Town September 1<sup>st</sup> 1794

Sir

I am this moment honored with your letter of the 25<sup>th</sup> ultimo.

The President has justly anticipated the feelings of my mind on the solemn occasion — I lament deeply the cause — I regret as deeply the necessity of resorting to the Bayonet to compel our fellow citizens to submit to the constitutions and laws of the people — But I also feel a thorough conviction of the justice of his conduct and hesitate not a moment in declaring my decision to afford my best support of his measures — Would to god it had been required on a Station better fitted to my talents and life important to our common Country — I should not then have experienced the additional pain which very keenly tortures me, from my knowledge of my inadequacy to the duties of the very responsible Station to which he has been pleased to call me. The high honor which his Resolutions always conveys, is extremely alleviated by the manner of his choice of me and fills my mind with the deepest gratitude. The best return I can make will be by the constant and zealous exertion of my humble Abilities in the line of my duty, and this I promise to do, and ardently pray that the Supreme ruler of the Universe will be propitious to my endeavors.

your letter of the 27<sup>th</sup> June, by Col. Walford, I received the tenth of August. The day after the Company met I received an Express from Capt<sup>n</sup> M<sup>c</sup> Calip, informing, that a Capt M<sup>c</sup> Cuskey from Georgia, who is famous for Such business, was warning men, and intended to attach them before they reached Pendleton, the Company immediately marched and Conducted them Safe. the Indians with the goods is now at the Courthouse. the last of the wagons with the goods only arrived two Days ago — I have recommended to Send Dinsmore to remain with the goods & Indians at the place where they are, till those who they are destined for, would be notified to Come down to the avenue to receive them. I have taken the liberty to recommend, as there is good houses to Store the goods, & as for the Indians not having to Shelter in — a runner was immediately dispatched to notify the Indians in the Nation of their arrival, not to lose no time in their Coming down to receive the goods at the avenue, with a recommendation to them to make, at Some Convenient place in their nation and Come even to either, and to Send avenues to us, to let us know three or four days before their arrival at the place where they are to receive the goods. Head Quarters
Miami Villages 20. Sept. 1794.

Sir,

I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 11. of July; and to enclose duplicates of my letters to you of the 14. & 28. ult<sup>o</sup>. also a copy of a second message to the Hostile Indians, which possibly may produce the desired effect.

The old difficulties of supplies still exist & ever will as long as they depend upon Contracts with private individuals: the enclosed duplicates of letters to the Contractors & Q. M. General will truly shew our disagreeable situation and which has been a continued source of difficulty & perplexity to me by ten fold more than contending with all the Savages in the wilderness.

General Barbee has this moment fortunately arrived with ten days supply of flour brought from Fort Recovery on the horses belonging to the Mounted Volunteers, the last particle that we had of that essential article was issued yesterday to the troops who have been for three six weeks past upon short allowance, or half a pound of flour p<sup>r</sup> man p<sup>r</sup> diem; and even at this moment we have but five days rations of meat in Camp without a particle of salt or a single drop of any kind of Spirits. however, I still hope to maintain my ground.

Permit me now to give you a short detail of our late manoeuvres &c. In my letter of the 14. ult<sup>o</sup>. I informed you that we had built a strong stockade Fort at the confluence of the Miamis & au Glaize, which I have since improved into a regular work surrounded by a good parapet sufficient to resist a twenty four pounder, with a fraize, projecting from the berm over the ditch, which is fourteen feet wide & eight feet deep — in addition to this, I have directed Major Hunt the Commandant to surround the whole to the water edge on each river with a thick abbatis that were ready cut and would require but little labor to compleat, agreeable to the enclosed draught: so that [underline: Fort Defiance] will support that name, even should the British & their Indian allies eventually attack it; nor can it be carried but by regular approaches, aided by a train of heavy artillery, which by recent intelligence are on their way to Fort Miamis.

The Legion was employed in making this additional work from the 29. ult<sup>o</sup>. until the 14. instant, on which day we took up our line of march & arrived at this place on the 17. cutting & opening a waggon road the whole of the distance being forty eight miles, the general course about W. S. W., without seeing an enemy or meeting with any interruption from them. How to account for the inaction or long silence I am at a loss — unless they are waiting the arrival of Governor Simcoe with the further reenforcement & heavy artillery, mentioned in the enclosed information given by a British deserter (& corroborated by three others directly) from Fort Miamis, before they ultimately decide for peace or war. Be that as it may, they are certainly sore from the late general interview with this army; nor can they support themselves but by the aid of the British Magazines, which probably cannot well supply from seven to eight thousand additional mouths including men, women and children now thrown upon them belonging to the different hostile tribes whose towns, & villages & provision are totally destroyed & laid waste & whose hunting grounds are now in our rear, so that their future prospects must naturally be gloomy & unpleasant.

48132:
War department

September 30. 1794

Sir

It is with regret I perceive by your return of yesterday that there is still a considerable deficiency of some essential articles for the Militia Army Knapsacks Canteens Musket Cartridges Blankets and shoes.

I am to request that you will press forward additional supplies of these articles as fast as possible to Fort Cumberland and Carlisle proportioned to the number of Militia to assemble at those places respectively Your object is to equip every man called for with one Knapsack or Valise one Canteen, one pair of shoes and thirty rounds of Musket Cartridges for every foot Soldier.

With regard to Blankets a number equal to half the whole number of Men called for will it is presumed suffice.

I observe that the Virginia Militia are still deficient in Camp Kells. It ought to be a primary object to make up that deficiency.

When you have completed thirty rounds for man of Cartridges you will forward an additional supply for the whole army equal to thirty rounds more by way of Carlisle and Bedford. The ammunition for the field pieces is also very defective. These ought to be at least thirty rounds apiece.

M<sup>r</sup> Francis has been directed to make a further provision of the foregoing articles except ammunition and also to provide a number of woolen Jackets and Overalls which are also to be forwarded with all possible expedition proportionally

proportionally to the before mentioned places. But after the 5 of October whatever is sent forward must take the route by Carlisle to Bedford. The supplies for the Southward therefore ought to be hastened on before that date. But no time should be lost in sending more ammunition to Carlisle.

You will also forward immediately one of the Boats, two thousand of the Overalls and three thousands of the Shirts you report to be on hand. Divide them between Fort Cumberland and Carlisle

I should be glad to have to morrow morning by 9 oClock a return of whatever you may have forwarded since the Return of yesterday.

It is relied upon that this instruction will be executed to the full extent. The Instructions you may receive from Cench Coxe Esq with regard to supplies till the Return of the Secretary at War are to be complied with.

You will on the 5 of October forward by express to Carlisle a return of all the articles which you send on not included in the Return you are requested to make to morrow and another by the post of Tuesday the 7 of October of every thing subsequently forwarded.

Nothing must be omitted to obtain with dispatch the means of transportation. All accounts prove that the Troops are a head of their supplies which is a very disagreeable circumstance.

With consideration and esteem

I am Sir

your obed<sup>t</sup> Servant

Alexander Hamilton

Sec of the Treas<sup>y</sup>

Samuel Hodgdon Esq<sup>r</sup>

Oct: 11. 1794]

Pha. Oct<sup>r</sup>. 11. 1794.

Sir

I have recd. your favours dated the 7: & 8: inst: & shall carefully attend to all your directions.

I find that owing to some neglect, your letter to the Bank of New york was not recd: a duplicate which I transmitted produced a cordial & prompt compliance; this accounts for a delay, which at one time I feared was owing to a reluctance to advance the sum requested.

It was not intended by me to intimate that Col. Nevil would act as Pay Master; he was engaged to take charge of the remittances to Mr. Williams & Genl. Miller & promised a compensation merely for that service.

The warrants for 90 M. D<sup>s</sup> for the pay of Genl. Wayne's army, have been issued & the notes made out. The Secretary of War will forward them to the army.

I have issued 50 M. D<sup>s</sup> for the pay of the militia army, which will also be sent forward as soon as possible. The Cashier of the Bank being indisposed, & a sum in small notes sufficient for the payment not being obtainable I fear some little delay. I have however advised the War Dept. to attempt an exchange of the large notes of the Bank of the U. S. for small notes of the other banks — this being the best thing that can be done under present circumstances & preferable to a remittance in specie.

I did not know that Mr. Gale was in want of money or it would have been furnished — he has however lately recd. 40 m. D<sup>rs</sup> & I presume has suffered no inconvenience.

I have issued 10000 D<sup>rs</sup> to Whelen & miller on a pressing application from Eli Williams for the transport service dated the 1: instant.

It was not possible for me to judge whether the 25 M. D<sup>s</sup> directed to be issued by you had been counted on, when Mr. Williams wrote — it may prevent mistakes & too great an expenditure if you adopt measures for combining the estimates for the provision dept. & Transport service into one view & requiring them to be addressed to you in person while you remain with the army.

I think that I may assure you that the means of the Treasury are adequate to any emergency that can be forseen at present.

I am with perfect respect Sir.
Yr. Obt. Servt.
O. Wolcott

Hon: Alex Hamilton Esq
at Head Quarters of the Army

Canandÿ. Nov. 15 1794—

Custom House,
Savannah November 17 1794

Sir,

I this day received your letter dated the 19<sup>th</sup> of September last, respecting a packet directed to John Mathews, esquire, Supervisor of the Revenue for this State, which was addressed to my care.

On referring to my letter book I find, that I notified Captain Constant Freeman of the receipt of the above packet as early as the 18<sup>th</sup> of June last, having been informed that it was to be forwarded to him by Mr. Mathews. This I learned from John Berrien, esqu<sup>r</sup>. (Mr. Mathews's Deputy and Attorney here) to whom I delivered the packet, and who supposing it might contain some Official Forms that would not be wanted in the upper Country, opened it and found that it was pay for the Troops to the amount of nine thousand nine hundred and eleven dollars. He thereupon requested me to take it back and deposit it in the Custom House iron chest until Mr. Mathews should send for it, he not choosing as his Attorney to risque forwarding it without his special order. Mr. Berrien wrote to Mr. Mathews acquainting him of what had taken place, and I requested Colonel Gaither, who was going to his station on the Oconee river, to inform Captain Freeman of it, that he might communicate with Mr. Mathews on the same. What prevented one or the other of those Gentlemen from coming or sending sooner for the packet I do not know, as they were both assuredly informed that it was in my hands; but it was not until some time in August that Mr. Mathews came to Savannah, when I delivered it to him. The Pay Master of the Federal Troops has since been here, and I gave him specie for a considerable number of post notes the same I believe that were transmitted through Mr. Mathews.

I am, Sir, very respectfully
Your ob<sup>t</sup> Servant,
John Habersham,
Cll<sup>r</sup>. of the Customs for Sav.

P.S. I have been and still am sick and confined to my room, therefore I should have forwarded my Accounts to the Department of War before this

Joseph Howell, Esq., Accountant to the Department of War.

48746:
By HENRY LEE, Governor of the Commonwealth of Virginia, Major General therein, and Commander in Chief of the Militia Army in the Service of the United States.

A PROCLAMATION.

BY virtue of the powers and authority in me vested, by the President of the United States, and in obedience to his benign intentions, therewith communicated, I do, by this my Proclamation, declare and make known to all concerned, that a full, free, and entire pardon, (excepting and providing as hereafter mentioned) is hereby granted to all and every person guilty of violations of the laws in Washington, Allegheny, Westmoreland, and Fayette, in the State of Pennsylvania, and in Berkeley, in the State of Virginia, guilty of Treason, or Misprision of Treason against the United States, or otherwise directly or indirectly engaged in the wicked and treasonable tumults and disturbances lately existing in those counties; excepting nevertheless from the benefit and effect of this pardon all persons charged with the commission of offences against the United States, and now actually in custody, or held by recognizance to appear and answer for such offences at any judicial court or courts; excepting also all persons avoiding fair trial by abandonment of their homes; and excepting moreover the following persons, the atrocity of whose conduct renders it proper to mark them by name for the purpose of subjecting them, with all possible certainty, to the regular courts of judicial proceedings, and whom all officers, civil and military, are required to endeavor to apprehend, or cause to be apprehended and brought to justice, to wit, BENJAMIN PARKINSON, ARTHUR GARDNER, JOHN HOLCROFT, DANIEL HAMILTON, THOMAS LAPSLEY, WILLIAM MILLER, EDWARD COOK, EDWARD WRIGHT, RICHARD HOLCROFT, DAVID BRADFORD, JOHN MITCHELL, ALEXANDER FULTON, THOMAS SPIERS, WILLIAM BRADFORD, GEORGE PARKER, WILLIAM HANNA, EDWARD MAGONER, PETER LYLE, HUGHES, DAVID LOCK, EBENEZER GALLAGHER, JOHN SHIELDS, WILLIAM HAY, WILLIAM MELHENNY, THOMAS PATTON, PATRICK JACK, STEPHENSON [undecipherable], JAMES BLAINE, ROBINSON, WILLIAM MCKINLEY, JOHN MOORE, and JOHN MCCOR-MICK, of Ohio county, in the State of Virginia.

Provided, That no person who shall hereafter wilfully obstruct, or attempt to obstruct the execution of any of the laws of the United States, or his or her wife aiding or abetting therein, shall be entitled to any benefit or advantage of the pardon herein before granted: And provided also, That nothing herein contained, shall extend, or be construed to extend to the remission or mitigation of any fine, forfeiture, or penalty incurred by reason of infractions of, or obstructions to, the laws of the United States for collecting a revenue upon distilled Spirits and Stills.

GIVEN under my hand, at Head-Quarters, in Elizabeth Town, this twenty ninth day of November, 1794.

HENRY LEE.

By order of the Commander in Chief.
G. K. TAYLOR, Camp.

Substance of General Waynes speech in answer to the Message sent by Isaac Williams given communicated by Jrancs who was one of the Party.

The General told the Messengers he was glad to see them come upon this business they did and at the same time pitied their condition in listening always to the English who wished to have them in the same Situation with themselves. They told them always to be strong and defend their Country, and furnished them with ammunition, but they might be convinced from their late conduct that they had neither the power nor inclination to help them. He had even employed the force of his little finger which they were not able to resist and dared not to fire at him, altho' under the Walls of their Fort. He advised them to retire to this side of the Divide, where they would be safe, as his young Men meant to range the plains this winter and destroy every thing that came in their way. Department of War, December 5th, 1794.

Sir,

The President of the United States has instructed me to transmit to your Excellency the enclosed Resolve, containing the unanimous thanks of the House of Representatives to the Militia in actual service for the suppression of the late insurrection.

The President having personally been a witness to the military merits of the embodied Militia, experiences the highest gratification in communicating this honorable approbation, the most precious recompence that could be offered to enlightened freemen. It is his devout hope, that the Militia of the United States, may ever be found to be the faithful and invincible protectors and vindicators of the great principles of Law and Liberty.

The citizens of America fixing in their minds as an indelible truth, that obedience to the laws, and the defence of their country, are sacred and indispensable duties, will render its freedom and happiness perpetual.

The President embraces cordially the present occasion, to tender your Excellency his sincere thanks for your zealous and powerful co-operation in the suppression of the late insurrection; as well for your exertions in calling out the Militia, as for your services in the field.

I have the honor to be,

With great respect,

Your Excellency's most obedient servant,

(Signed)          H. Knox, Secretary of War.

His Excellency Governor Mifflin.

TREASURY DEPARTMENT,
Revenue-Office, *December* 26, 1794.

SIR,

I HAVE had the honor to receive, this day, the order of the House of Representatives, relative to the measures that have been adopted concerning the naval armament, in your letter of the 10th instant.

It was on the 4th of April that the correspondence with you in the Treasury business for the War Department, was committed to this office.

After the frigates were determined on, the timber to be procured, advertisements were issued on the 16th of April, for the live oak and cedar timber, reviewed by the Secretary at War; as also on the same day, for cannon ball, twenty-four pound cannon, and Kentledge or iron ballast; on the 7th of May advertisements were issued for the yellow and pitch pine and white oak materials, and for the locust treenails; and inquiries were made for ascertaining into the terms on which the cordage could be procured.

Many other enquiries were likewise made, but no contracts or purchases were or could be completed before the 9th of June, the legislature not having granted until that time, funds for this purpose. On the 16th September of the day (the first moment when it was legal) an agreement was made with John T. Morgan, a master shipwright and timber merchant of Savannah, for the purpose of procuring, in concert with persons in that place and in Savannah, the live oak, red cedar and pitch pine materials. His business was to search for the timber, to superintend the cutting, and forming it by the moulds for the frigates, and to procure it to be rafted, for floating from the swamps, to where the frigates were to be built. It was further agreed, with the consent of the Secretary at War, that he should be employed to build a frigate at Charleston, if any should be built there. By the concurrence of both departments, he was to be allowed pay at the rate of two thousand five hundred dollars per annum of claims of Services, and expenses in the Carolinas and Georgia, or while building. Like this, all the principal contracts were made, as you well remember, in concert with you, after the necessary conferences from time to time.

*The* Secretary *of* War, *in obedience to the orders of the Preſident of the United States, ſubmits to the Houſe of Repreſentatives the following report reſpecting the Frigates authorized by the "* Act to provide a naval armament.*"*

THAT the paſſing of the ſaid act created an anxious ſolicitude that this ſecond commencement of a navy for the United States, ſhould be worthy of their national character. That the veſſels ſhould combine ſuch qualities of ſtrength, durability, ſwiftneſs of ſailing, and force, as to render them equal, if not ſuperior, to any frigates belonging to any of the European powers. Reſearches therefore have been made for the beſt principles of conſtruction; and ſuch proportions adopted as have appeared beſt, upon the moſt mature advice and deliberation.

The largeſt ſhips, of forty-four guns, will be conſtructed upon a ſcale to contain thirty cannons, of the caliber of twenty-four pounds, upon the gun-deck. The others, of thirty-ſix, twenty-eight cannons, of the ſame caliber, upon the gun-deck. The remaining force will be made up of twelve pounders and braſs howitzers.

The frigates will be built of live oak and red cedar, in all parts where they can be uſed to advantage. Theſe valuable woods afford the United States the higheſt advantages in building ſhips; the durability being eſtimatd at five times of the common white oak. Beſides theſe woods, the beſt white oak, pitch pine, and locuſt, are directed to be uſed in the conſtruction.

Expedients have been deviſed for ſeaſoning the plank, as expreſſed in the letter of Joſhua Humphreys, herewith ſubmitted.

But the procuration of the live oak and cedar (being of ſouthern growth) has been retarded by the circumſtances ſpecified in the letter of the Commiſſioner of the Revenue.

The building of the ſhips has been directed in the ſeveral following parts of the Union, in order as well to diſtribute the advantages ariſing from the operation, as to aſcertain at what places they can be executed to the greateſt advantage—to wit.

One thirty-ſix, at Portſmouth (New-Hampſhire).
One forty-four, at Boſton.
One forty-four, at New-York.
One forty-four, at Philadelphia.
One thirty-ſix, at Baltimore, and
One forty-four, at Portſmouth or Norfolk (Virginia).

The following arrangement has been adopted for the building and equipment of the frigates.

1. All contracts for the principal materials of conſtruction and equipment, have been made in purſuance of law, under the direction of the Secretary of the Treaſury.

2. All labour, and inferior materials not otherwiſe provided by the Secretary of the Treaſury, are to be procured by agents, whoſe compenſations are two and an half per cent. conformably to their inſtructions hereunto annexed, marked No. 1.

3. The captains of the frigates are to ſuperintend the conſtruction and equipment in purſuance of their inſtructions, No. 2.

4. The conſtructors or maſter-builders, are to be regulated by their general inſtructions, No. 3.

Department of War
December 31. 1794

Sir,

Your several Letters have been received. No more money can be expended upon the fortifications, until Congress shall appropriate the same by Law. It is most probable that the fortifications of the principal posts will be carried on with a view of permanency. Until however their decision is known, you will be considered as in ferme upon your former rate of payment also the Assistants under you not appointed heretofore by me.

The Works must be placed in the best possible Condition, so as to be uninjured by the Winter Season —

It has been understood that the Works in Georgia have languished for want of an Engineer. M<sup>r</sup> De Grasse, at present in Charleston, has been mentioned as a suitable Person to act as an Engineer. His father has rendered great Services to the United States and this appointment would be convenient to this Gentleman. I have therefore appointed him at the rate of two dollars and a half p<sup>r</sup> day —

You will endeavour that he shall work under your [undecipherable] direction.

I am
Sir
Your obedient Serv<sup>t</sup>
Knox

Sir

I am highly gratified by the receipt of your letters, public and private, of the 4.<sup>th</sup> and 5.<sup>th</sup> ultimo, which reached my hand on Christmas day —

You will naturally believe, that Sensations of Singular pleasure, have been excited in my breast, by this annunciation of the Sentiments of the President, in a case which deeply interested my Honor and my repose —

And to you Sir, my warmest acknowledgements are due, for the polite and friendly terms, in which you have been pleased to make the Communication —

I have long waited in anxious Solicitude, for the Presidential decision on my

my requisitions & Statements of the 30.<sup>th</sup> of June, which had rendered my Situation a delicate one, and highly interesting: I am now amply compensated for my inquietude, by the justice and Wisdom of the award; and I feel Conscious, that So long as my conduct is conformed to the inclinations of the executive, that it will be approbated by the Virtuous, and remain invulnerable to the Shafts of Malevolence. —

I unfeighnedly believe, that the wishes of the President of the United States, are as safe for my Guidance, as any Law in morals, and it follows, that no Suggestions of Conciliation could spring from Him, to leave my honor dubious —

It is therefore Sir, and from these considerations only, that I consign the past to oblivion and make a peace offering, to the New Year, of my dissaffection, my Mortifications & reprehension —

To these motives of dutifue respect to the inclinations of the President, paramount to all others, might be added, the present Circumstances of the Legion, dispersed in such extent, by furloughs, Patrols, & detachments, as to render the assembly of the Officers, essential to the inquiry, or the prosecution difficult, dilatory, and manifestly injurious to the public Service; the Grave too has robbed me in the persons of Major M<sup>c</sup> Mahon and M<sup>r</sup> Robert Elliot, of much important testimony; yet Sir, I stood prepared for the conflict, and the specific acts of misrule embraced by the General Charges alledged against Major Gen<sup>l</sup> Wayne had been committed to paper anterior to the Commencement of the Campaign —

But Sir, whilst I avow my preparations & my readiness for a Candid inquiry, I can most conscientiously declare to

to you, that no man possesses a stronger indisposition to controversy, than myself, I abhor discord from whatever Source, because it imbitters every hope, & blasts every day; it is the mortal foe of human happiness, wayslays every generous Sentiment, and robs it of its Commission —

If I know myself, my Country cannot boast an officer more Solicitous to guard the profession of Arms, from the pollutions of dishonor or to enlarge the boundaries of Friendship —

The Scene which, at my Sole instance, ensued in the Cantonment of Greenville on the 3.<sup>d</sup> of November when at the head of the Officers of the Army, I waited on the General, and in their behalf complimented & Congratulated him, on his success & personal good health, is an illustration of the Sentiments which I cherish —

My Lips are now Sealed; my Pen is dismissed from depicting well founded grievances

and I implore Heaven, that the painfull office may never more be forced upon me — with high consideration, & great respect — I have the Honor to be

Sir

49094:
[Report of David Robinett. acting as Deputy Collector for the District of Delaware respecting the Ship Jumeaux Captain Rualt.]

December 31. 1794, Agreeable to orders given to me by George Bush Collector of the District of Delaware I proceeded to Port Penn in the revenue Barge and on January 1. 1795, went on board the Revenue Cutter, General Greene, commanded by Captain James Montgomery, with Thomas Rothwell the Deputy Marshal, and Captain Dale of the Militia with about forty men, we proceeded down the Bay as far as Bombay Hook, where we found the Ship Jumeaux laying at anchor.

The Cutter then hove too and made to the Ship. The Deputy Marshal, Captain Montgomery, Captain Dale, Ensign Van Dike and myself boarded the said Ship in the cutters boat, and found her to have no more Guns than what appeared she cleared out from Philadelphia, viz: 4 fix pounders, but they were mounted on old carriages. and two swivels, harpots were opened for 18 guns, with ring bolts &c. and appeared to have about 40 men on deck (and it was believed a number more in the hold) she was deep waisted, near five feet high in her waist, and well found; as soon as we boarded her, the commanding officer was asked, if the ship was called the Jumeaux and if his name was Rualt, to both of which questions he answered in the affirmative. The Marshal and myself made known to Captain Rualt that we were civil officers of the United States and by virtue of Authority to us given for that purpose, do now seize the Ship Jumeaux, for having violated the laws of the United States, by contravening our neutrality, and demanded the Captain forthwith to return with his Ship to the port of Wilmington to stand trial. Captain Rualt after much hesitation and equivocation submitted reluctantly, and promised to carry the Ship back - and he accordingly weighed anchor, and flood up the Bay about three miles; soon after the Pilot named Joseph Pruspel, in consequence (as it appeared) of threats from the crew, and the command of Captain Rualt, as it was in French, bore away the Ship, and flood down the River again. Captain Montgomery ordered the Pilot to alter his course and stand up the River, he said he dare not act contrary to Captain Rualt's orders.

Captain Montgomery took hold of him to send him on board the Cutter, upon which several of the crew seized him and by force and violence detained him; Captain Montgomery then hailed the Cutter and ordered her to keep close on board, upon which there was an immediate cry of citizens to arms, and the Boatswain also piped to arms; Captain Montgomery knocked the pipe out of the Boatswain's mouth for which he was very much insulted; so much so he had to lay his hand on his sword, and after which we were all treated very rude and insultingly. They immediately manned their cannon, and brought them to bear on the Cutter and run into the round house for their arms; Captain Rualt said he could not command his men, that they were determined to go to sea, and would not return; night approaching it was thought most advisable to leave the Ship (though the Marshal wished to stay all night) The Captain said he would not sail that night, but would come to an anchor, which he did - we accordingly returned to the Cutter and not having a sufficient force to stand her cannon without sacrificing a number of good Citizens and perhaps to no effect, we returned to Port Penn about 10 o'clock that night. The next day Major Grantham put as many men on board the Revenue Cutter as she could carry, and got a small Sloop with the remainder of the troops on board and the Revenue Barge, with a determination to board the Ship, we got under way and proceeded down the bay, but could not find the Ship; She had taken her departure with a fair wind and was out of sight.

We then returned to Port Penn, and the troops were ordered to their respective places to be dismissed.

David Robinett

Wilmington Jan.<sup>ry</sup> 5. 1795.

N.B. The Boatswain a Frenchman and four of the men took the Ship's boat the night after we left the Ship and made their escape he says they were discovered just as they left the Ship; the officers ordered some of the passengers to fire on them (as they said they were all passengers) but none would fire, he reports they had ninety five men on board and plenty of ammunition, the Ship he said got under way about 9 or 10 o'Clock P.M. the night after we left her.

D.R.

T.D. Jan<sup>y</sup> 19<sup>th</sup> 1795

Sir

I have rec<sup>d</sup> your letter of this day. The estimate of the sum requisite for the Jersey Militia greatly exceeds what I had supposed to be necessary. There are two dangers attending so considerable advances on account without adequate data to guide — One that a good deal more money may be issued from the Treasury than is necessary with the inconvenience of a difficult & perhaps dilatory after reckoning — the other that persons not intitled may be paid, or that those intitled to something may be paid more than they ought to receive.

Now the Men are disbanded it seems to me right that future advances should be made on grounds, which are as certain as the nature of the case admits.

This is my idea, however, I will, if you require it, put into the hands of the Treasurer, the sum asked for subject to your Warrant, if you inform me, that it is your wish.       With great respect I am

Sir Y<sup>r</sup> Ob<sup>t</sup> Servant
A Hamilton

West Point, July 9<sup>th</sup> 1795,

Sir,

I enclose an account of contingent expences with its vouchers — also my account for salary to the 31<sup>st</sup> of last December. — No person could have taken more pains than I have, in laying out every farthing of the Public monies that went through my hands, to the best advantage for the Public.

Capt<sup>n</sup> W<sup>m</sup> Scott informed me the 26 of last month that his agent gave him advice his pension was established, and added that after that day he should not act as an Ajutant. I was very glad to hear it. The next day he set out for Albany. He owes me 15 dollars & 15 cents, for which he gave me his note of hand. He told me he expected daily from Philadelphia, a considerable sum of money, out of which on his return he would pay me & others he owes. As a security, in case of his death, for part of what he is indebted to me, he left in my hands his account for his salary to the 20<sup>th</sup> of last January with a receipt for it, amounting to 57 dollars & 33 cents. He expected to return here in three weeks from the day he departed.

I have to solicit you will do me the favor to retain in your hands, out of his salary and pension, to the amount of what he owes me, until I inform you of his having paid me.

Previous to his receiving his last pay of 57<sup>d</sup> which he owed me 149½ dollars — I mentioned to you in my letter dated the 3 ultimo how it happened he got the money from me. On my not letting him have an opportunity to get more of me, and refusing to let Doctor Lawton, who borrowed money of me, have more, they were both monstrously disappointed I should use them so ill, as the termed it. —     My last letter was dated the 21 ultimo. —

I am, with consideration,

Sir,

Your most obedient,
Humble servant,

Geo. Fleming.

Joseph Howell Esquire. —

This affied to the an expensive business, both with respects to Salt & repacking. In the article Pork, it is not pointed out in the Contract whether any part of the Carcass is to be rejected in packing. Sir,

When orders were given for using only live Oak in certain parts of the frigates, that part which is here distinguished by the name of [underline: Dead Wood] was not mentioned; because it was apprehended that live oak of the size requisite for that use could not be obtained. To this you will be pleased to attend. Captain Dale will undoubtedly return from China in full time to take command of the frigate to which he has been appointed.

The superintending of her while building may be committed to Captain Samuel Barron as soon as he returns from Sea, and in the interim to his Uncle Captain Robert Barron. Both are of Norfolk, experienced Seamen, and recommended by the Agent M<sup>r</sup>. Pennock and others. Samuel Barron is a candidate for a first Lieutenancy in the Navy, and will feel a peculiar interest in performing attentively the Office of Superintendent. Captain Dale will compensate them for the services they render in his stead.

Under these circumstances I have thought it would be expedient, that Captain Dale should be indulged with a furlough during the time necessary for performing his intended voyage to China: otherwise an Officer so universally and highly valued and esteemed will be forever lost to the naval service of the United States.

On communicating the matters here stated to General Knox, I have the pleasure to find his opinion entirely concurring with my own.

Should the reasons, Sir appear satisfactory to you, I shall beg to be honored with your determination as early as may be convenient.

Captain

Philadelphia 25 March 1795

Sir.

I have received the books, intitled the Element and practice of Rigging, and Seamanship &c which you did me the honor to send me, a few days ago. I have only had time to run over them in a cursory way but if you will be kind enough to leave them with me, for the present, I will take them to Baltimore and at my leisure there, examine them with attention, and if I find any thing new or worth communicating, will commit the same to paper and make the most early report to you. From what I have seen however in these books, there appears nothing more than a collection from different Authors on various subjects relating to Marine affairs, but on a more particular examination of them, it is possible, many matters may be found well worth our investigating with attention; as I conceive nothing to be of more consequence in the equipment of a Ship of War, than her being well masted and spar'd. I have examined what M<sup>r</sup> Steel, the author of the Collection in question, says on that subject, and have made out two setts of the principal Spars, agreeable to the principles he has laid down. the one for our forty four Gun Frigates and the other for three of thirty six Guns— They are here enclosed and marked A. I am of opinion, that candid, and competent Judges, when they compare

compare it, Steel's dimensions, with those laid down by me, in the book I have lately published, will consider mine better adopted for our Ships of War, than his, and I think the Author of this Collection also produces arguments to prove it in his second Vol. Chap. VII, page 273. — "The correct height for the Masts of Ships, is still a problem which remains to be solved by the Builders; The most skillful of them, have not paid attention enough, to the solutions, and determinations, which are contained in the works of the late M<sup>r</sup> Bouguer on that subject; it seems on the contrary, as if they had endeavoured to deviate as much as possible from the true principles, in that respect, by raising the Masts a great deal more than they were formerly, although they were already much too high, as the learned Author I have just mentioned, has asserted, and experience confirmed by repeated observations has convinced me of this truth. Viz<sup>t</sup> that as soon as a Ship inclines her velocity diminishes in proportion as her inclination increases; this principle has been verified on different vessels, and at different times, by several Officers and in various oblique courses." I do myself the pleasure to send you four of my books— one for the War Office and one for each of the Ships to be built at New-York, Boston, and Portsmouth, Newhampshire— The Ship here and there to the Southward, I shall furnish each with one. I thinks Sir, it would be well to take the opinions of Cap<sup>ts</sup> Nicholson, Talbot,
in

in writing, and require their observations on Steel, and my dimensions, as also the opinion of their respective Builders, Cap<sup>t</sup> Barry and M<sup>r</sup> Humphreys being on the spot, can be consulted at any time. As I have quoted a part of M<sup>r</sup> Steel's remarks on masting, which is against his own System, I submit to you, whether a copy of the same or this letter, had not better be sent to the above Gentlemen.

I purpose calling on you, in a day or two, respecting some alterations, necessary to be made, for the better regulating of the Navy Yards.

I have the honor to be Y<sup>r</sup>

[signed] Thomas Truxtun.

I have rec<sup>d</sup> your letter of the 8<sup>th</sup> with your account for a quarters pay, includ commencing the 1<sup>st</sup> of January last. This letter contained the first information of your accepting the appointment of Clerk of the Navy yard at Boston; &tho the general rule to make the date of the acceptance the time for commencing the pay. But in your case if you omitted declaring your acceptance till after you entered on the duties of your Office, then your pay may begin with the commencement of your Services.—

I observe that you have calculated your pay at 70 dollars a month; the fixed pay is 62½ or 750 dollars a year. This cannot be exceeded. I must therefore wait for your answer before your pay can be remitted.

Two points you se remain to be determined. first the day on which your pay ought to commence. the 2<sup>d</sup> one whether your acceptance is under the idea of acquiescing in the Sum allowed to every other person in the same Station. 750 dollars a year. — The usual, I may say the universal mode of paying Public Officers in civil departments, is at the end of each quarter of a year. It may not be convenient to make the single exception in your case.—

The building of the Frigate being a Temporary employment, I wish it may not prove permanently detrimental that you have thrown aside your private business. Whether an attention to the latter would have been compatible with the former I cannot have but it merited consideration when the question of accepting or declining the appointment was before you. I mention this because I must tell you candidly that representations of hardships or of sacrifices by engaging in this species of public Service cannot be admitted as grounds on which to claim higher compensation than others receive for the same Service.—

War Office April 28. 1795.

Sir,

I have received your letter of the 22<sup>d</sup> inclosing the copy of a letter from General Biggs, informing of some hostile act of the Indians on the border of the Ohio. The appointment of scouts may therefore be very proper. By the last Western mail I received a letter of the 8<sup>th</sup> ult<sup>o</sup>. from General Wayne, by which it appeared, that altho' [underline: all] the hostile nations, in that quarter had entered into a capitulation for treating of peace, ney, June & casing hostilities in the mean time, yet that there was a predatory party of Cherokees (and probably the bandetti of some other tribes,) collected, or rather making their quarters, on the Waters of Sciota, from whence they annoyed the frontiers: but he had sent to them a message by a Shawanoe Chief, threatening their destruction if they persisted in their hostilities now that the [underline: Nations] had stipulated a suspension

of all hostile acts, & for making a general peace, and that Chief promised to aid the General in extirpating that banditte, if they persisted in their depredations.

I had not before heard of the killing of a man at the mouth of Little Kenhawa. The man killed on the Sciota ought not to have been there. The western papers have informed us of a party of hunters falling in with some Indians not far from Wheeling — but the hunters were in the [underline: Indian] [underline: country] — that is, on the northwest side of the Ohio, on the hunting grounds which have been the very object of this fatal Indian war. I am suspicious that this is the same party of hunters to which General Biggs refers. If so, I say of them, that they ought not to have been there.

The President is now in Virginia. On his return your letter shall be laid before him.

I am with great respect,
Sr, your most ob<sup>t</sup> Servant
Timothy Pickering.

War Office  May 2. 1795.
Sir,

I received your letter of the 22d. — If he was fairly inlisted, an exchange would be inadmissible, merely because he had repented.

The recruits confined at Norwich I suppose are the same of whom Governor Huntington lately wrote to me. I answered, that they could not be retained, if under age, and the parents or masters demanded them. The service of a minor is the property of his parent or master; and without a special law ought not to be taken from them, but by their consent. In ordinary times, like the present, such a law certainly will not be provided.

As you appear to be recruiting successfully, I am satisfied that you should continue in that place; and I trust all your exertions will be made in it. But your recruits must be marched immediately to Middletown, where with the recruits at that place they must be embarked for Brunswick New

New Jersey. It will <sup>be</sup> advisable for you to go with your recruits and to deliver them to Captain [undecipherable] who will have orders to take the command of the whole. Those with you, if recovered and fit for duty, should march with your recruits to the Legion.

I depend on your executing these orders with despatch. Peace will undoubtedly be made with the Indians, who are to assemble at Head Quarters at Greenville next June for a general Treaty: but the ranks of the Legion are thin; and we must show a respectable military force.

I am, Sir,
your ob't servant
Timothy Pickering

P.S. Let the recruits be made as comfortable as possible with the cloathing on hand. Deficiencies will be supplied here; and other cloathing now run for future recruits. Do not keep a man who is able to march. One of your music must go with them.
— Captain William Eaton

I am D: Sir with esteem your

h<sup>ble</sup> servant
Theo Lyman

War Office May 11. 1795

Sir,

I received your letter of March 23 on the 21 of April — Having written fully on the subject of hostilities between the Chickasaws and Creeks in my correspondence with Governor Blount and anticipated your enquiries, it was not necessary again to answer them. I have no doubt that as you [underline: intimate], those hostilities have been precipitated on the part of the Chickasaws by men who sought neither their true interest nor the interest of the United States. Governor Blount has been informed that the United States cannot support the Chickasaws, and I think satisfactory reasons have been given him for refusing it.

Money to pay the expences incurred the last year in the South western Territory was forwarded by Mr. King of Knoxville who left this soon after the departure of Major Evans.

I have now to inform you that goods to the amount of about three thousand dollars, will go off this week (perhaps to morrow) for Pittsburg, whence they will go with little delay down the Ohio and up the Cumberland to Nashville, for supplying the Chickasaws according to a voluntary promise made to their Chiefs who were last year in Philadelphia. To whom should they be delivered at Nashville as the public Storekeeper?

The Secretary of the Treasury has formerly written to you about the storing and issuing Indian supplies at Knoxville. As far as the circumstances will admit the like <sup>mode</sup> should be pursued at Nashville. But quere whether the quantity of supplies will render it worth while to have a special Storekeeper, who shall issue on the orders of the Superintendant General Robertson? You have the means of knowing characters there will be able to determine. The Superintendant for the Six Nations receives and issues himself all the supplies to those Indians. We have a perfect confidence in his integrity. The like supplies to the amount of three thousand dollars is annually to be furnished for the Chickasaws.

I shall write you again on this subject, in the mean time you will think how the business may most properly be conducted and consider this letter as confidential.

I am
Sir
Your humble Servant

sign<sup>d</sup>. Timothy Pickering
Secretary of War

Col. David Henley

The subject of the letter and March 13. 1795. from Harry Innes Esq<sup>r</sup> of Kentucky, to the President of the United States, with the letter of James Smiley inclosed therein, has been considered by the Secretary of War; who now respectfully reports to the President —

That in the letters of the late Secretary of War, the accounts of the Service of scouts [strikethrough: directed] were to be certified on oath, by the County Lieutenants, or Commanding Officer of each county. The accounts thus certified were to be presented to the Paymaster of the United States, who was to pay the amount to the County Lieutenant or Commanding Officer of the county, who was to pay the individual Scouts & take their receipts. That all such accounts as have been so made up and presented, are presumed to have been paid to the county Lieutenants or other officers commanding in their stead. Whether the sums so advanced have by those officers been paid over to the individuals, is not known at the war-office; those officers not having settled their accounts.

The answer given by M<sup>r</sup> Howell to M<sup>r</sup> Smiley, if in the form represented by M<sup>r</sup> Smiley, was improper: indeed so very improper as to excite a doubt whether M<sup>r</sup> Smiley's memory was correct in repeating what he supposed was spoken. M<sup>r</sup> Howell recollects no such thing. But if the reprehensible words were uttered, the only satisfaction M<sup>r</sup> Innes can receive will arise from the information that M<sup>r</sup> Howell is no longer in office.

Navy Yard June 22, 1795.

Sir

I have to observe on M<sup>r</sup> Fox's letter to you, dated Naval Yard, Portsmouth, June 9. 1795 that neither time nor expence should be spared in laying the keels of the Frigates in the best possible position for launching. I think from his description of the ground, it will be very proper to lower the keel a base in fact, to keep it as low as possible on the blocks, all fore and aft, as will barely admit of putting on the false keel. If they have sufficient water for launching, I would give the Keel the same declivity as the Launching ways. If the water is scant, it should be left as described in a former letter to you on that subject.

(signed)    Joshua Humphreys

In framing the bows of the tenders, a regular plan must be adopted, but the roots cutting in many of the top timbers of one leave two bills of timber nearly together, in many places and a short piece will be standing in the body of the third futtock to reach the keel son, in order to prevent these evils I find from the manner of these timbers in the 44 Gun Brigs &ca that it will be necessary to alter from the heads and butts of the timbers.

Timbers in the body may either run up as short tucks the timbers will admit of. The roots probably have a long or short top timber both of which can be on the wake of the root.

As there appears a difficulty in procuring the top timbers of 44 Cedar, I am bold enough to those of the timbers that are marked in the bottom to cut the parts to be of Red Cedar, because they can the more easily gets then if they were to be of the whole length, all the top timbers and half timbers that form the sides of the ports should be both live oak and as the little that is in the wake of the chain should be of the same by butting the timbers that cut for the masts of 44 Gun Brigs, to admitting as near as possible with the general direction of having as far of the tall timbers of Red Cedar, some of the top timbers proved — off being straighter than those given, shaped as nearly possibly the best to be done — it being be proper to put their in where they do not interfere with the ports &c, &ca —

The 44 Gun Brigs perhaps may not be cut more than afore taken for the moulded — Their numbers may be sent to the Builders for the 30 Gun Brigs, &ca, the butts of the timbers they, after mould, be taken from the Draft —

50324:
[Copy of a Letter from James Hackett Naval Constructor Portsmouth, N.H. to the Secretary of War — May 29<sup>th</sup> 1795.]

[Sent to Joshua Humphreys Esq<sup>r</sup>. June 5. 1795. for his use.]

[signature/initials]

Portsmouth N. H<sup>o</sup> May 29 1795

Sir

I received your letter of the 13 instant, inclosing M<sup>r</sup> Humphreys letter of 31<sup>st</sup> December 1794, & February 7. 1795, also yours of the 19 instant with M<sup>r</sup> Humphreys letter of the 16 instant and his table of the timber of the Frigates, I have observed the contents. I have ever been of the opinion that the scantlings of the timber for the 36 Gun Frigates were to large, & am happy to find M<sup>r</sup> Humphreys ideas in reducing them coincide with mine, also I think the transoms & fashion pieces are too heavy, and if reduced in the moulding, the upper fashion pieces sided two inches thinner, it would take off a weight from the Stern, which as it now is will be a strain to this thin part of the Ship. The main transom does not work to the dimensions, it being very veiny and somewhat defective, and will not moudle more than twenty inches, nor side more than nineteen. The second and third transoms are both breeched & small heart-streaks appear in the middle and on the backsides of them all. The first futtocks side to the dimensions, and part of the second also. The third futtocks will not side more than eleven inches to get them straight. The sternpost will not work to the dimensions at the head by an inch, so as to make it any way square. In my opinion the Gun deck beams sided and moulded according to the dimensions given for the Frigates of 36 Guns are too large in proportion to other ships of war. For an English Ship carrying 100 Guns, the lower deck beams are moulded eighteen inches and sided the same. For 90 Guns the beams are moulded sixteen & one quarter inches, & sided seventeen. For 70 Guns the beams are moulded sixteen & half inches and sided the same. For 60 Guns the beams are moulded 15¾ inches and

and sided fifteen inches.

With deference I would offer as my opinion that if the Gun deck beams for the Frigates of 36 Guns were sided sixteen inches and moulded fifteen, they would be full strong enough for the Ships, as they will be so near together. To have one beam under every Gun port except the hatchway and one between each port will leave but little space for the ledges and knees. To have the beams of the dimensions which I have submitted they may much easier be got whole and free from sap or veins.

I find that some of the largest of the live oak timber is defective and shaken, which is generally the case with all large timber. If it will not do to cut out the small defects & put in sound wood we must condemn a number of timbers, which I should suppose might pass.

Cap<sup>t</sup> Sevier the Superintendent has been very particular respecting the timber which would not side to the dimensions; but they work only as large as before mentioned, and as they sided and moulded very square at that, I think the Ship will not be the worse, altho' the upper timbers sided from an half inch to an inch smaller than the dimensions.

I have no objection to sawing & boring the beams, but our beams being hewed out, and will probably lay for some time in salt water, I think it must penetrate thro' them, that the sawing perhaps will not be necessary & if the beams are cut fit to put into the Ship, it will be best to

to pay the ends with hot tar and burn it in, boring two holes within two feet of the end obliquely to come out at the distance of twelve inches from the end, and within two inches of the bottom of the beam, and within two inches of being thr[ough], fill up the holes with oil, & as often as it soaks away, until the waterways must be laid down; then bring them up being full which will penetrate to the ends of the beams, and in my opinion will preserve them better than salt, as salt is very destructive to iron.

As building Ships of live oak timber with us has never been practised and not knowing the nature or durability of it, leads me to observe, that I wish M<sup>r</sup> Humphreys opinion on feiring the timber where it is found defective, as many valuable pieces must be lost if the practice of feiring cannot be admitted. A piece of live oak timber apparently sound often when sided discovers a shake and may be repaired with some timber on this plan.

It appears to be requisite to reduce the copper bolts as first proposed, which can be done in this place.

I received an order on Joshua Wentworth Esq<sup>r</sup> Supervisor at Portsmouth dated September 4<sup>th</sup> 1794 for 500 dollars which was duly paid & shall be much obliged you would order what is now due me, to be paid as soon as convenient.

I am Sir with respect
Y<sup>r</sup> obedient Servant
Signed        James Hackett

The Honble
Timothy Pickering
Sec<sup>y</sup> of War
