Navy Yard - June 5. 1795 -

Sir

Since writing the foregoing Received Col Hacketts letter, the foregoing part of which is answered in that of Cap<sup>t</sup> Severs. The Main Transom, a principal piece and should be without defect. it should not be put, if it was a good piece and something smaller than directed, it might be best dispensed with. I am great Friend to large Transom, there should be no danger of weakening it from cutting large holes for the Heels of the [undecipherable] Timbers in order to give good Hold- and Security— The Objections that were stated to the Strength of pine Beams was one cause why they were not made one Inch larger than at first intended— If Colonel Hackett should add one inch to the Beams sideways as stated by him— Suppose they would do very 13 by 17. and if he is to put in oaks I would advise [undecipherable] the way he mentions, in order to Ascertain which is the best mode— I am well satisfied the Timber I have now worked agreeably to the directions are in a good proportion for their particular Stations, and for No 1 the Size of the 44 Gun Frigates—

Col Hacketts observations are very just, with respect to defective Timber many timbers may be lost if it should not be admitted to for— those are matters I suppose ought in great degree rest with the Constructors and Superintendants, as it is almost impossible to draw the line, however they should be cautioned against putting any bad timber—

M<sup>r</sup> Cheesemans letter of 20 of May, he mentions the propriety of having —

Signed Joshua Humphreys —

50443:
To Captain William Eaton.

The Congress of the United States having made a provision for carrying on trade with the Indian Nations on our borders; and the President having determined to establish a Trading post at Colerain, on the river St. Marys, in Georgia, for the purpose of supplying the Creeks and other Southern Indians with goods, it becomes necessary to provide for the protection of the establishment.

The disorders committed on that frontier, whence inroads have been made into the adjoining Spanish territory, in violation of the laws of the United States, and of the rights of a neighboring nation; and the just apprehension that the like or other outrages may be attempted, by a set of people who disregard all legal restraints, [strikethrough: & spare not] [undecipherable], require that a military force be employed, as well to aid the civil authority in bringing to justice the persons who have perpetrated the enormities above mentioned, as to prevent future aggressions, and to preserve peace and order in that quarter of the United States.

The preserving of peace between the frontier inhabitants of Georgia and the Creek Indians, by protecting each against the malicious or vindictive designs of the other, is a third important object. Unfortunately the necessity of some further provision in this case has recently become manifest. Seventeen Creek men, some of them known to be great friends of the white people, and all coming to that frontier with peaceable views, have been basely and cruelly murdered. Such at least is the conclusion authorized by the intelligence

received from Georgia.

To these several objects your particular attention must be directed. You will be diligent in your endeavours to train the troops under your command to an expert discipline, & to have them always in readiness to execute any orders relating to these objects.

A law of the United States passed on the 5<sup>th</sup> of June 1794, having declared "That if any person shall within the territory or jurisdiction of the United States begin or set on foot, or provide or prepare the means for any military expedition or enterprise to be carried on from thence against the territory or dominions of any foreign prince or State with whom the United States are at peace; every such person so offending shall on conviction be adjudged guilty of a high misdemeanor, and shall suffer fine and [undecipherable] imprisonment at the discretion of the court in which the conviction shall be had; so that such fine shall not exceed three thousand dollars, nor the term of imprisonment be more than three years:" And the same law having also authorized the President of the United States or such other person as he shall have empowered for that purpose, to employ the force of the United States to prevent the carrying on of any such expedition or enterprise: I am to inform you, by command of the President of the United States, that you are hereby empowered to employ the force under your command for the purpose aforesaid, to prevent a repetition of outrages against the Spanish dominions. The Attorney General has this honor of Stating his opinion upon the question proposed to him by the Sect of War, viz: Whether the State of New York has a right to purchase from the Six Nations or any of them the lands claimed by those nations and situate within the acknowledged boundaries of that State, without the intervention of the general government.

By the Constitution of the United States, Congress has power to regulate commerce with the Indian tribes, and by the act of 1 March 1793, it is expressly enacted, that no purchase or grant of lands, or of any title or claim thereto, from any Indian or nation or tribe of Indians, within the bounds of the United States, shall be of any validity in Law or equity, unless the Same be made by a treaty or convention entered into pursuant to the Constitution, that is to bill be a commissioner or any person not employed under the authority of the United States in negotiating Such Treaty or convention directly

[Address: His Excellency / The Governor of Pennsylvania]

[War Department]

War Office June 20. 1795

Sir,

The President of the United States has referred me to your letter of yesterday's date, forwith his instructions, anticipating the necessity of permitting troops in the present service of the United States to make the more permanent Establishment at Presque Isle. I wrote last week to Col. Butler at Pittsburg, to fix his eye upon an officer suitable for this particular command. I could then do no more, not having consulted the President. He now consents to the measure contemplated; and by this day's post I shall send orders for marching the troops which I propose to assign for that service. When completed, I mean that they should be able to make the establishment independent of the assistance formerly expected from the State of Pennsylvania.

Col. Biddle has informed me that provisions for four months for the troops intended to have been raised by the State have been transported to Le Boeuf. I shall depend on these supplies for the troops of the United States now to be ordered to Presque Isle.

I am very respectfully

Yr. ob't servant

T. Pickering

June 27<sup>th</sup> 1795

Sir

You having entered into Bond faithfully to discharge the duties of Pay Master to the Kentucky Volunteers — conformably to Instructions which you were to receive from this Office.

You are requested strictly to observe the following: — to wit

1<sup>st</sup> As your accounts for service of the Kentucky Volunteers in 1793 have not yet been settled, and entered to your Credit on the Books of this Office — owing to payments being made contrary to your instructions from this Office of 7<sup>th</sup> May, 1794 — The Vouchers produced by you being in part illegal by Payments being made to sundry Persons — who sign themselves attorneys to the Soldiers without the Power of Attorney accompanying the receipts; and owing to deficiencies in Vouchers — You are without delay, to proceed to the State of Kentucky and on your arrival here apply to the Batallion Pay Masters who have any monies to account for either by illegality or deficiency of Vouchers — and make a final settlement — making an Account Current, and entering therein the money you paid them, and the amount expended by them for which legal Vouchers must be produced and the Balance of any remaining in their hands is to be returned to you — The arrears then due to Individuals in their Battallions are afterwards to be paid by you to those Individuals or their Attorneys duly authorized to receive the same — The Vouchers on which the payments are to be made are the receipts of the Individuals for their pay — Payment
50605:
may be made on well authenticated Powers of Attorney — they expressing it to be for the use, and benefit of the individual.

3<sup>d</sup> The Accounts for monies in 1794 being now adjusted and the amount having been paid into your hands.

You are to proceed therewith to the State of Kentucky without delay— on your arrival there you will take the most effectual measures for the speedy payment of the monies to the Individual Claimants— The Vouchers on which these payments are to be made is as before directed— The Receipt of the Individuals or a Power of Attorney well authenticated and expressing it to be for the use and benefit of the children— The monies due to deceased Soldiers are to be paid on Legal Letters of Administration or duly authenticated Copies thereof which with the Receipt of the Administrator are to accompany your Accounts as Vouchers for your payments.

It being the opinion of the Secretary of War, that all your accounts in Kentucky may be settled on or before the 4<sup>th</sup> of April next ensuing— it is expected that no exertion will be wanting on your Part to effect the same, and that you will attend at this Office on or before the first of May with all the Vouchers properly arranged, and an Account Current— Stating the monies you received and expended for each charge regular Vouchers are to be produced, and the Balance remaining on your hands as to be refunded to the Treasurers of the United States.

Sam<sup>l</sup> Hi V<sup>C</sup>
William Simmons

New London June 27, 1795.

Sir,

I have the Honor to transmit you a Muster Roll & Pay Roll of the Recruits inlisted by me, made up to the Commencement of the present Month.

By the Circular letter of the Accountant of the War Office, dated March 1, 1793, I am directed that on transmitting each subsequent Bill of Muster Roll, the Vouchers for the Expenditure of the Sums previously remitted & must accompany the same. Some of my Men having been absent it was not practicable to complete the Receipt Roll, in order to their being transmitted at an earlier Season.

They are accompanied by my Recruiting Account made up to the End of the present Month, together with the Voucher for the Sums already expended & a Statement of the Balance due.

At the Time of transmitting my former Account, I had not received the Voucher for the Bounty paid to Joseph Burke by Sergeant Clark amounting to ten Dollars, which you can now examine. As I have thought myself bound to pay it to the Sergeant I conceive [undecipherable] it ought that it should be allowed to me. Should there be any Doubt, a Detail of the Circumstances shall be communicated.

I have ventured to address your Office the Bill of Expences incurred in pursuit of Deserters from this Rendezvous instead of the Secretary of War, to whom I am directed by the Articles of War, judging it to belong to your Department. The Vouchers are inclosed.

West Point, July 1<sup>st</sup> 1795

Sir,

Agreeably to the instructions, which I have received from Colonel Rochefontaine, I transmit to you, for the month of June, 1795, a muster and pay roll of the Second, third and Fourth battalions of the corps of Artillerists and Engineers. — That one general fund might be established, from which might be issued the pay of all monies due to the corps, I have been directed to include every officer of the three last battalions, although they may be detained on duty, which may not admit of their being from present at this garrison; but as I could obtain no return of the men under their respective commands, I have been obliged to omit in the roll all the noncommissioned officers and privates, not now on duty at West Point.

I have also been directed to request that you would send me printed receets, musters, and pay rolls; and transmit an account of balances due to the officers of the Second, Third, and Fourth Battalions. — The officers present have requested me to represent respectfully to you, that they experience inconveniences in not having the arrears of pay, due to them on former muster rolls, transmitted to this garrison.

I would Sollicit from you Such further information, as you might Suppose requisite to promote order and regularity in the Paymasters accounts. —

I have the honour to be with great respect,

Sir,

Your most obedient Servant

Mh. Freeman

The Accountant of the War Department

Freeman Pay master of the Regiment is Sending to you the Muster Roll according to the formation of the three battalions for the month of June: we will endeavour to Set the Comptability in the greatest light and order. I request you Sir to forward to the Council of Administration the Sum which is due for the past month of June according to the Muster roll and an equal Sum for the month of may. which is also due and which the pay master will pay to the officers and Soldiers according to the Muster Rolls which have already forwarded to you.

Newport 9 July 1798

Sir

This will be handed you by Capt Elliott, to whom I beg leave to refer you for our opinion respecting the fortifications necessary to be erected for defending the town and harbour of Newport and also for estimates of the same according to the best information we have been able to obtain.

There are mounted on Sea coast carriages at Fort Wolcott three eighteen and three twenty four pounders and we are in want of four twenty four pounders more which will be the complement for that fort, and I estimate the expense to complete the fort exclusive of the purchase of Cannon at One thousand dollars. I think that orders might be given to employ thirty men immediately on Fort Wolcott and I will give all the aid the weak state of the Garrison will admit of.

Two forts in addition to Fort Wolcott we conceive to be indispensibly necessary at this place — One to be erected at Brenton's point and the other on Tommorary hill but before we break ground I give it as my opinion that some more able Engineer should be sent to give the plan.

We further propose that four light eighteen or twenty four pounders be mounted on travelling Carriages for the use of the Citizens and to be used as Circumstances may require —

I have the honor to be &
signed W<sup>m</sup> Littlefield
Cap. Commandg

James McHenry Esq<sup>r</sup>
Sec<sup>y</sup> for the department of War

Sir

Since writing to you on the 7. June I have received information, the truth of which is not to be doubted that the Spanish government have actually erected a Blockhouse, a Stockade fort and planted Cannon at the Chickasaw Bluff upon the East

Past bank of the Mississippi within the limits of the Territory, unless the Governor of the Natchez was himself present at the erection of these works as appears by the information of several white people who saw and spoke to him, one of whom he informed that he was determined to keep up a garrison at that place — He came up the river with three ladies which continued opposite to the Bluff until the materials for erecting the Blockhouse were prepared, upon the West side of the river brought over to the East side, and the Blockhouse, Stockade &c erected all which was done with great haste. The Chickasaws have applied to me as your Excellency will see by William Glover's letter of the 12 June herewith forwarded, to move the Spaniards from that place. To this request I can give no answer until I receive your Instructions as to what I shall answer, which I presume I am not to get until you shall have reported the movements of parties to the President and receive his answer —

I have the honor to be with great respect
Your most ob<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup> [signed] Robertson

His Excellency
Governor Blount

By the arrival of Cole Rochefontaine on the 15<sup>th</sup> Instant I received your letter of the 2<sup>d</sup>.

I shall endeavour by every necessary attention to facilitate the works intended at Presqu'Isle or any intermediate Posts, and in order to give all possible assistance, and to forward the Transportation of the Stores from Port Franklin & Laboeuf I have concluded to accompany the Cole to Presqu'Isle, if we have determined to set off on the 20<sup>th</sup>. I find it necessary to take this Journey as well to facilitate the transportation as to receive the Stores & Provisions now at Laboeuf & to provide for their being deposited at Presqu'Isle.

General Wilkins has agreed to deliver Eight Thousand Rations of the Provisions now at Laboeuf on the terms of the Contract with the State of Pennsylvania. This deposit at Laboeuf will remove any difficulty in the way of immediate supplies of Provision at Presqu'Isle as neither French Creek or the Allegheny are Navigable.

All the Goods for the Treaty have been sent forward, & I suppose those last sent are at Fort-Washington.

New London July 25, 1795.

Sir,

The letter which you did me the Honor to address to me on the 14 current has been received, and I have attended to the Objects referred to in it. By Inspection it will appear that I have included in the Muster Roll all my Recruits, distinguishing however those who were detached to Westpoint. I preferred this Method because they did not leave the Rendevous untill the last Day of June which completed a Month since the former Muster.

You will I suppose have received a Muster Role for the Month of June transmitted by me on the 11 current. One of my Men who had been out in pursuit of Deserters, and whom from his long Absence I had considered as a Deserter has since come in. To prevent any Embarrassment I have made out the Muster Roll anew in which he is returned as missing. I therefore request that the former Muster Roll may be cancelled.

The Account of Serjeant Blonks Expences inclosed, with his Vouchers, will shew the Grounds of my paying the Sum of 3<sup>k.</sup> [undecipherable] to him as charged in my contingent Account.

The Pay Rolls for myself & the Men remaining with me is made up from the Time of the last Settlement to the 1<sup>st</sup> of the current Month inclusive. I am Sir respectfully your obed<sup>t</sup> Servant

Decins Wadsworth Cap<sup>t</sup> in the Corps of Artill<sup>y</sup> & Engineers.

Sir

I have received your letter of the 11<sup>th</sup> instant from Saint Simons. I have expected that you would direct the construction of the Frigate to be built at Norfolk, but your present in procuring timber for all the Frigates is indispensable. I must therefore entreat you to continue in your present employment, until the timber is all garnered. Then you may return to Norfolk. In the mean time what timber has been or shall be sent to that yard will be hewed and fashioned for the work, under the direction of a very able temporary naval architect M<sup>r</sup> Fox who assisted M<sup>r</sup> Humphreys in preparing the draughts and moulds. But as it has been determined to throw the full quantity of timber into the yards at Philadelphia, and Baltimore and afterwards to supply the other yards among which Norfolk may be the last, so the construction of the Frigate there will principally rest under your direction. This plan I hope will be agreeable to you.

50969:
War Office July 31. 1795.

Sir,

The Governor of New York, in pursuance of a law of the State, has requested the President of the United States, to appoint a Commissioner to hold a treaty with the St. Regis Indians, to afford to New York an opportunity to extinguish their claims to lands in the northern parts of that State. The President assents to the measure, and tenders to you the office of Commissioner, which I hope the situation of your affairs will permit you to accept. The time proposed by Governor Jay for holding the treaty is about the middle (not later) of next September. He writes me that he shall appoint three agents on the part of the State to negotiate the purchase of the Indians. The place of treaty is to be Fort George, at the South end of Lake George.

I request your speedy answer, that if any circumstances should prevent your acceptance of the office of Commissioner it may be time to make other application.

I am very respectfully,
Sir, your ob<sup>t</sup>. Ser<sup>vt</sup>.
Timothy Pickering

Jeremiah Wadsworth Esq<sup>r</sup>.

Sir

The Bearer Jesse Crafts has to day applyed to me for pay for military Services performed in the year 1791. I have refused him to give note because you have the money in hand to pay him, but that you may understand the nature of his demand & State it to the War office to the end that the money may at Some future day be forwarded to you.

The facts respecting Crafts demand are that he was a Lieutenant in Major Rheas Battalion of Levies raised in this [undecipherable] in 1791 and marched North West of the Ohio — Major Rheas Battalion consisted of four Companies three of them actually marched North of the Ohio & were there mustered and Since their return to this Territory have been paid by D<sup>r</sup> David Allison the Fourth commanded by James Coopers whose Lieutenant M<sup>r</sup> Crafts was never crossed the Ohio & so it has happened that Cap<sup>t</sup> Coopers, his Subalterns & every other part of his Company yet remain unpaid by the United States for their Services

I presume upon your forwarding a Copy

Sir,

I inclose to you for the month of July, a muster and pay roll of the corps of Artificers and Engineers at West Point; by which there appear due for that month, to the corps at its garrison one thousand, eight hundred and seventy two dollars, and thirty six cents, exclusive of what may be allowed to such part of the Staff of the corps, as have not yet had their pay made up. I have calculated in this roll, agreeably & my instructions, the pay of the deserters to the date of their elopement.

I have received your letter of the 25<sup>th</sup> ultimo. It informs me, that the balance of one dollar and one cent is, as I have stated in my recruiting account current, due to the United States. You will have observed,

that there are due to one of the men, whom I have inlisted and who is now present at West Point, the bounty of four dollars. If you will transmit to him two dollars and ninety nine cents, and order me to pay him one dollar and one cent, I will send you his receipt for the amount of bounty due; or if more agreeable to you, you will deduct one dollar and one cent out of my monthly pay for July. In either case, you will be pleased to exonerate me from the charges, now standing to my debit, for monies placed in my hands for the recruiting Service.

I wrote you in some haste on the 4<sup>th</sup> instant to explain a difference which will [strikethrough: not] appear in the number of men on the muster roll, I now send you, and the number on the monthly return made out on the 1<sup>st</sup> of August by the adjutant, and transmitted the last post, by the commanding officer, to the Secretary of War.

I have the honour to be
with great respect,
Sir,

Your most obedient
very humble Servant;

Paymaster &c.

Westpoint August 7<sup>th</sup> 1794

Sir

The pay master of the Regiment forwards to you by this post the Muster Roll for the pay due to the Corps for the month of July. — I request you Sir, to be so kind as to pay a particular attention to the two articles which we Submit to the decision of the Secretary at war viz a temporary provision for the pay master's clerk and the Same for the attendant in the hospital — by the muster rolls, the pay and receipt rolls which are to be kept double, you may judge that an officer who at the Same time is charged to record the proceeding of the Council of administration & of the correspondance with you would have a very little time to give to learn the duty of an Artillerist and Engineer if he was not allowed a clerk to assist him; the clerk must have also a provision for that trouble — as to the

attendant in the hospital, this Subject needs no recommendation.

I Suppose that the Secretary at war is often Busy, So I apply to you to desire earnestly that you would obtain a temporary decision on these two petitions and a speedy answer upon it — if the Secretary is willing to place Confidence in the members of the Council of administration they could debate it and pay them out of the Contingency money in the chest till the provision being made, at which time we Should lay our claim to have the money refunded in the Regimental chest.

with great esteem
I have the honor to be

Sir
Williams Simmons Esq.          Your most obedient
&                              & humble Servant

Lewis Toussard

Inclosed I transmit you a Muster Roll and Pay Roll for the months of June and July, I have still inserted James Boyar (who was taken by the Civil authority) as I have some expectation of getting him again, the circumstance will be determined before next muster — I have also inserted John Smith as it was in June that he was discharged, until which time he received pay — John Reader who is hear in confinement, deserted from Maj. Roberts when he was a Captain and Recruiting in Charleston — Augustine Lopez who I have put in the bottom of the Muster Roll, deserted from Fort St. Tammany on the River St. Marys in the State of Georgia, was taken in Charleston and Confined here, but having no convenient place, he in a few days made his escape — I have for this some time past been laboring under a severe indisposition but hope soon to recover so far as to be able to expedite my Accounts — I have also inclosed you a Duplicate of a Letter I had the honor of writing you on the 23 July, the original of which and its inclosures, I hope you have received —

I am Sir

your most Obt.

Fort Johnson July 23. 1795

Sir

I wrote you on the 27<sup>th</sup> June inclosing Muster & Pay Rolls up to the last of May — I now transmit you Receipt Rolls and receipts for the pay of Officers and Soldiers who where paid by me; should there be any irregularity, I hope you will make an allowance as it is the first, — I have accompanied them with an Account Current, and stated the ballance that remains in my hands — The ballance taken from the Receipt Rolls will amount to twenty Cents more then is stated in the Account Current, which the Receipt Roll for July, August, & September, amounting to three hundred seventy eight Dollars fifty three Cents will specify, but the letter accompanying the same from the former Account mentions only three hundred seventy eight dollars thirty three Cents which was the amount of the money I received for the above mentioned three months; I did not suppose it of Consequence, but as there appeared a difference in the ballances, I took the liberty to mention it — I have in possession Duplicates of the Receipt Rolls and receipts inclosed, except Lieut. I am Sir

with respect

your most Obt.

Hbl. Sevt.
Michael Patterson
Capt. &c. —

Philadelphia 24 Aug<sup>t</sup> 1795

Sir)

It, accidentally happened that your Letter of the 21 Cur<sup>t</sup>. did not reach my hands, until this Morning. —

In the ordinary Course of Communication, I could not yet, expect Answers to the Letters I wrote Cap<sup>t</sup> Hame and to the Kings Vice Consul at Newport, immediately, upon the Receipt of those I was honor'd with, from the late Secretary of State, of the 15 Cur<sup>t</sup>. — a little Time will, I trust, put me in possession of the means of entering into a satisfactory Explanation. — I look forward Sir, with some Degree of Certainty, to a Confirmation of all the Facts, I have ventured to suggest. —

I have anticipated the Expectation of this Government, as to the Medium thro' which — Representations in Cases of Injury or Insult, are to be made; and I feel as Gratification in the Confidence, that Instructions will be given to the respective State Governments, to secure the Rights to which his Majesty's Commanders in common with the Officers of other Neutral Nations, have an Unquestionable Claim: But which [without recurring, unnecessarily, to past Causes of Complaint] have not, in some particular States, heretofore, been regarded, with that Alertness and Respect, which the impartial Principles of Neutrality prescribe:

In the present Instance, I am persuaded this Government will pay due Consideration to Acts, which, may probably, have originated in misconception, where there is a total Disavowal of Insult intended to the Sovereignty of the Country; and to Expressions of Resentment, which have resulted alone from a Sense of Injuries — wanton and reiterated, and of Malevolence the most Mischievous — and inhuman.

The slow progress of the Dispensations of Justice, can administer but a weak and ina[dequate] Relief for Injuries, which have lately come to my knowledge, against which, I may have occasion to remonstrate; and unfortunately local Distances preclude the Interposition of the general Government, with that Dispatch, which Cases of sudden Exigency require. —

I am thankful to you for the Communication you have been pleased to make to me, of the Resignation of the late Secretary of State; and shall avail myself of your obliging permission to address my Letters to you until I shall be apprized that a Successor is appointed. —

With Sentiments of Consideration and Respect,

I have the Honor to be,

Sir,

(Your most obed<sup>t</sup>.
and most h<sup>ble</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>.

P. Bond

West Point, August 25<sup>th</sup> 1795.

Sir,

M: Hagner's Letter of the 18<sup>th</sup> instant has come to hand, and has been laid before the Council of Administration.

I have paid the troops, who arrived at this garrison in the months of June and July 1795 to whom arrears of pay were due on the 30<sup>th</sup> of June last; But I shall not transmit to you the rec<sup>vt</sup> roll till I am enabled, by the arrival of money, from New York, to pay also Captain M: Creis detatchment to that date.

I have the honour
to be with respect

Sir,

Your very humble Servant

Neh. Freeman
D. Paymaster at West Point

William Simmons Esq<sup>r</sup>.

I am, Sir,

your ob<sup>t</sup> Servant

51249:
Navy Yard 21 August 179[5]

Sir,

I have considered Col° Claghorn's letters of the 9th July and 7th of August, with attention, am of opinion that if none of the timbers were less than the directions, sideways, they may be put in the ship, if in every other respect they are good and not too great a deviation from the dimensions, in these I would recommend discretionary power with M° [undecipherable]

The objections that were stated to the strength is, pine beams, were in cause why they were made one inch larger than at first intended: the dimension of the pine was never altered for the Oak, and as reducing the size of the Oak will tend to durability, I conceive there will be no impropriety in making them 15 by 17, which is only half an inch larger than Col° Claghorn wishes, the others in the same proportion.

(signed) Joshua Humphreys

The Hon<sup>ble</sup> Timothy Pickering Esquire.

[Mr Josiah Fox / Norfolk, Virginia]

Portland Sept 19. 1795

Sir

I enclose you the Muster roll & pay roll of my recruits for the months of July & August together with vouchers for the balance of the sum remitted for pay of the recruits till the 20<sup>th</sup> of June last. — Two causes have conspired to delay me in transmitting the vouchers — incidental delay in drawing the money from the Supervisor, & the necessity of sending to West Point for Ebenezer Thompson's recpt.—

I have ventured to include Joseph Cole on the pay roll, deducting the time he was absent by desertion. Thirteen Dollars & eleven cents were expended in apprehending & securing him & John Cole, his brother. You will probably be able to determine whether this sum ought to be deducted from their pay. Should that be your opinion I suppose half of it should be stopped from Joseph's pay. — I have, however, inserted what I conceived to be his whole pay from the time I formerly mustered him.

John Cole yet remains in custody of the civil law. It is very obvious, that he was [underline: rescued] from me, merely to prevent his being sent back to West Point. His [underline: nominal] creditor now avows it to be his intention to hold him confined during the term of his inlistment.

It is my intention to send Sergt. Moses with Joseph Cole, Abner Cole & Tristain Cole to Capt. Foye, to be by him forwarded to West Point; as the Captain informs me he has several recruits whom he wishes to forward thither. This circumstance will lead you to cause their pay to be sent on as soon as possible after the rolls shall have come to your hand.

I am, with respect,

Sir

your very obedient servant.

[underline: D. H[undecipherable]le Lt. A.&E.]

William Simmons Esq<sup>r</sup>.

Philadelphia 3<sup>d</sup> Sept<sup>r</sup> 1795. 149

Sir

I have this moment received your Letter of this date. I take the earliest Means to inform you that I have not been so fortunate as to receive Answers to Letters, written to Cap<sup>t</sup> Hame and M<sup>r</sup> Moore; so long ago as the 17 & 18 Ult<sup>o</sup>. — And having had no Intimation of the late Circumstances, to which you allude, but from very vague and, I am convinced aggravated Reports, I can form no Judgment of the Operation they may have had upon the mind of the President of the United States in accelerating any Measures, the President may contemplate in Respect to Cap<sup>t</sup> Hame.

If it be deemed improper to suspend the Determination — I trust I shall be apprized of the Tendency of the Measures, as soon as may be consistent with your convenience, that I may take the earliest Opportunity of making the proper Communications to his Majesty's Ministers.

I think it necessary to observe to you, that I have, by repeated Letters, endeavour'd to ascertain the real Truth of this Case — : I feel therefore conscious that I have done all that was incumbent upon me to do : That I have fulfilled in Point of Respect what was due to your Representations and that I have discharged the Obligations I owe to his Majesty's Officers — whose Conduct is implyed in your Representations — : I can then, only, lament Sir, that any Accidents should have delayed the Explanations I have every Reason to expect, upon the receipts of Letters from Newport; — which I understand in the ordinary Course of Communication I ought to have been in Possession of many Days ago.

With sentiments of Consideration and R[espect] I have the Honor to be Sir

Your most obed<sup>t</sup>
hbl<sup>e</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup> —
P. Bond

Department of State Sept 5<sup>th</sup> 1795

151

Former communications from this Department, have expressed the intentions of the Government to wait a reasonable period, for such explanations of the conduct of Cap<sup>t</sup> Rodham Home, Commander of the British Ship of War, Africa, and of M<sup>r</sup> Moore, the British Vice Consul at Rhode Island, as they might think proper to offer, relative to the injuries against the rights and dignity of the United States, which were the Subject of those communications: That reasonable period has elapsed, and no satisfactory explanations have been given — I have it therefore in command from the President of the United States, to inform you, that the eventual measures announced to you, respecting Cap<sup>t</sup> Home, will now be taken; together with such others as his subsequent aggressions against the United States appear to demand; and of which the inclosed protest of John Tillinghast — George W. Page — Samuel Almy — and Daniel Young, will give you informations.

Cap<sup>t</sup> Home will, therefore be required to remove from a Station within the Jurisdiction of the United States, where he continues to violate their Rights. He will be required to liberate three Seamen whom, within that Jurisdiction, he has, unlawfully, seised — and after forty eight hours from the time) these requisitions of the President shall be communicated to him, all intercourse between the Ship, under his command, and the United States will be forbidden.

I am further to inform you, that Thomas W<sup>m</sup> Moore Esq<sup>r</sup>, his Britannic Majesty's Vice Consul, at Rhode Island, having cooperated with Cap<sup>t</sup> Home in the injuries heretofore preferred against the Government of the United States, and the Chief Magistrate of one of them: — The president has thought fit to revoke the Exequatur heretofore granted, to the said Thomas W<sup>m</sup> Moore, who is no longer to exercise the functions or powers of a Vice Consul, within the United States. —

These Proceedings of Cap<sup>t</sup> Home and M<sup>r</sup> Moore are considered by the President, as the unauthorized acts of individuals Officers, and that they will not interrupt that harmony and good understanding; which it is the Disposition of the Government to cultivate and maintain, between the two Nations.

I am Sir with great consideration
Your ob<sup>t</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup>

51371:
Springfield 8<sup>th</sup> Sep. 1795

Sir,

Ensign Remington is in a deplorable situation — Intemperance has reduced his health, and imprudence his credit — His creditors have arrested his body at the same instant that I was reduced to the necessity of ordering him in arrest — He is in close confinement, with friendless moneyless and without credit —

From the use he has made of recruiting money which I have put in his hands I do not feel safe in trusting him further — If his arrears of pay could be forwarded he may probably extricate himself from civil arrest, refund the bounty money, and have means to get to his connexions which I consider the fittest plan for him; for wherever it is, the public will never be benefitted by any service he will ever under—

It is painful to make this statement; but they are facts which cannot be trifled with — The man who had the address to obtain En<sup>s</sup>. Remington's appointment merits no thanks from his country; for it was notorious that dissipation and debauchery had rendered him unfit for public service or confidence — So soon as his pay arrives I shall take the liberty to discharge him, that his patron may have the pleasure of his society till he is bold to leave or obtain leave to resign —

I am very respectfully Sir, your
Obedient & very humble Serv<sup>t</sup>.
William [undecipherable] Cap<sup>t</sup>. [undecipherable]

Sir

Upon favour of the 8<sup>th</sup> Instant is received.

The box of Stationary by the hands of Edw<sup>d</sup> White is arrived, Jno. By what means the Letter of Capt Home and the other papers (you mention) were made public, I am ignorant. But their publication is no proof of partial resentments — against British subjects. Philadelphia 12 Sep<sup>tr</sup> 1795

Sir,

I have the Honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of this Date, inclosing Extracts of a letter from his Excellency Governor Fenner of the 5 Inst.

I do not feel that I am called upon to make even an indirect Reply, to any observations, applied to me, in the Explanation that Gentleman has been pleased to Offer — relative to his public Conduct; I think myself fortunate, Sir, that the Course of my Official Correspondence is to flow in another Channel; my Communications upon every Subject, which relates to my Nation, are to be directed to the Appointments established under the General Government, from whom, having, on my part, always manifestly the most unfeigned Respect, I have in return, experienced great personal Civility.

The Tenor of my Official Correspondence with the late Secretary of State, and with you since his resignation, relative to very sudden and unexpected Events, has clearly Designated my solicitude to avoid every Interruption of Harmony and goodwill; — Upon the Subject of Complaint I was very imperfectly informed — upon the other, I was in possession of a direct Canvass walk of the charge, which I communicated to you, unofficially, I am ready to admit, as that it came to me, unofficially. —

Whatever else I have collected, concerning the existing Charges, has been from very loose and uncertain Rep[orts] and so I have freely Declared; "Why I have been dep[rived] of the means of making a full explanation, even at t[his] moment, is, yet, to be accounted for.

Two Things I may venture to Assert withou[t] The one, that the Governor of Rhode Island has with[held] a Statement of Facts, explanatory of one part of Capt R[ow's] Conduct, which was couched in Terms Temperate a[nd] concilliatory — The other, that his Majesty's Vice Con[sul] at Rhode Island, has incurr'd in very pointed Cens[ure] from this Government, before he was even called u[pon] to refute or explain, the specific matter which attracted [its] Censure.

Another thing I have from a sense of its [ill] Tendency, very seriously Lamented; the publication [of] Official Correspondence, while matters are in a Trai[n of] Negotiation — A practice which you must allow to b[e] productive of great Inconvenience; tho' you seem t[o] think it was unavoidable, in the recent instance [of] which I have complained. —

With Sentiments of Consideration and Re[spect]
I have the Honor to b[e]

Sir

The expence however of two scouts to each of those counties will be so inconsiderable as to create no difficulty. The latter I will transmit to the President, and await his determination. It is proper, in the mean time that I inform your Excellency, that peace is made with all the Indian tribes on the frontiers of all parts of the States. Even the district of Mero on Cumberland, so long the scene of depredations, is now enjoying perfect tranquility. I have not yet received an official account from General Wayne but the quarter master general wrote from Head Quarters on the 3<sup>d</sup> ult. to his deputy at Pittsburg (from whom I received it) that on that day the treaty was concluded with all the Western Indians. I cannot but hope therefore that the recent orders of [undecipherable] recalled very speedily. Nothing is to be feared except from a few scattered ruffians whom no general pacification can disarm. Sir,

I am directed by the Secretary of War to transmit you the following extract of a letter from Ensign Charles Martin dated "Carlisle September 13. 1795 " I am Sorry that I have occasion to mention the Clothing again for my Recruits "and am at a loss how to account for their delay as M<sup>r</sup> Richard Parker informed " me he had them packed up when he was in Philadelphia in July last. I "have several Recruits in a very bad condition without a shirt to their backs "or Overalls or in short any article of clothing there not being one single "Garment of any kind at this post"

On examination I cannot find any order for forwarding clothing to Carlisle since the fourth day of May last at which time a request was made that twenty five suits might be sent to that place — Should that order have been complied with — you will please to have transported to Carlisle as expeditiously as may be an additional supply of twenty five Suits —

I am
Sir
with great Respect
Your obedient Servant
H. Jones
By Order

The purchasing materials at the very lowest price for cash in hand Col<sup>d</sup>. [undecipherable] informs me he wants for building & repairing the artillerists quarters, and the hiring the number of carpenters & masons at the most reasonable wages he also informs me he wants for the same purpose, and satisfying myself they, and the laborers earn their wages, is all that comes within my province relative to the disbursements of the public monies. I assure you I take the greatest precaution to prevent being imposed upon in what I do.

I expect in a few days Col. [undecipherable] will be able to spare a number of the masons from the houses to secure what was done at Fort Putnam last year — This is [undecipherable: probable reading "specially"] necessary, to keep the money from being lost that was laid out on said fort. As soon as he can spare carpenters, I will set them at work to repair the ordnance storehouses & the powder magazines, agreeably to directions I received from the Secretary of War — these are, I have been for a number of years in a deplorable condition.

There are hired & employed here 23 carpenters, 6 carpenters' apprentices & 13 masons. Of the artillerists artificers there are 29 that draw a half ration each & day for working — The chief of these I suppose would not have inlisted had they not had an aversion to working. I will pay particular attention to what you mention relative to my vouchers. There is not a voucher I have sent since I have been here but I can have properly authenticated. —

You will now receive a packet of vouchers for contingent expenses with an account of them, amount 3616 dollars & 85 cents — and receipts from the detachment of the legion here for their April, May & June's pay, amount 267 dollars.

My being out of public money prevents my arranging a number more of vouchers I have, in time to go by this mail. I will send them at the end of this month to make a settlement.

I have requested the hon. the Secretary of War to forward to me immediately for contingent expenses at this garrison six thousand dollars. — I will thank you to let me know the general heads I am to keep my disbursements under. The business I have to transact is so complicated, I find a great difficulty to keep them even as I do at present. I am, with great respect

Sir

Your most obedient

Sir,

The Packet of Newspapers [undecipherable] arrived by this days Post but not accompanied by a letter from you as usual. I mention this circumstance because you intimated in your letter of the 5<sup>th</sup> Instant, that you intended a remittance by this days Post.

Colo Butlers Estimate of Cloathing for the Troops now at the upper posts & Recruits expected amounts to upwards of two hundred Suits including Non-commissioned Officers & Musicians.

The First hours you have to spare from your Official duties and Amusements, I have to beg of you to devote to this particular service of your friends. The public Service requiring the utmost œconomy should take place in the Naval Yard at Gosport, Virginia I take the liberty of recommending the following regulations to your notice, in adopting which the public Service will be considerably benefited by the provision and Stores that will be saved thereby —

1<sup>st</sup> I would recommend to keep M<sup>r</sup> William Herbert, as director or Builder of the Yard during M<sup>r</sup> Morgans absence, as he is a Man of abilities and Integrity that whatever Stores shall be received at the Yard may be hauled up and properly Stowed —

2<sup>d</sup> to have the Keel [strikethrough: properly] securely covered from the weather, and the outer part of the Ship (which is at present unfinished) to be completed —

3. not to admit of any additional Buildings to be erected at the public expence there being sufficient buildings already erected to hold the Stores to be used in Building said Ship —

4. to discourage the Workmen from Sleeping in the yard, frequent quarrels having hitherto taken place —

5<sup>th</sup> the Clerks office to be kept in the yard, either one of the rooms over the [strikethrough: undecipherable] may be appropriated to that purpose, or at the North end of the Barracks —

6<sup>th</sup> the Clerk of the Yard is to attend strictly to his Duty — not to interfere with the Constructor's Business, but to assist him in all [underline: Respects] conformable to his instructions, and to take care of all Timber and other Articles that may be brought to the Yard, previous to their being used in the Construction of said Ship whether they lye in the Water or Otherwise and take particular care they are not Stolen or broke adrift, and when his leisure will permit he is to go amongst the Workmen and see they are diligently applying themselves to their several Occupations, he is also to do what the Constructor may deem necessary —

7<sup>th</sup> the Clerk of the Yard to keep daily Account of the Provisions and Rum served out to the Workmen, that no unnecessary waste may be made, and to make [undecipherable] Returns of the same —

8<sup>th</sup> Workmen to be allowanced in provision and Rum agreeable to M<sup>r</sup> [undecipherable: probable reading "Penn"] and M<sup>r</sup> W Herbert [undecipherable: probable reading "Spencer"] — to which the Clerk will conform —

9<sup>th</sup> that all Requisitions for provisions and Rum shall be made to the Agent at least 48 hours before the same shall be wanted — as frequently happens the wind and tide prevents the Boats going to Norfolk —

51678:

[To]

Your letter of the 19<sup>th</sup> Ultimo was transmitted to me and received at Presqu'isle on the 2<sup>d</sup> Instant consequently tho' not the Sooner of acknowledging the receipt of it as early as might have been expected.

Found it necessary to accompany Col<sup>o</sup> Butler to Fort Franklin in order to assist him in Carrying out the buildings now erecting at that Place — We set off from this post on the 22<sup>d</sup> Ultimo &arrived there on the 25<sup>th</sup> and immediately fixed on a convenient situation at the Mouth of French Creek for a block house the lower Story of which is to be appropriated as a Store House — Barracks for an officer and twenty men was also then laid out and is in considerable forwardness these buildings are to be enclosed with a Stockade: Materials for which as well as for the building is almost all procured & I expect the whole will be nearly completed at the end of this month. Shortly after my arrival at Fort Franklin I found it necessary to proceed to Presqu'isle in order to ascertain what additional Means of Transportation for the Supplies of that post might be necessary. Found a considerable part of the road from Buffalow to Le Boeuf cut off to almost the road from Le Boeuf also greatly impaired — a team of eight Good Oxen not being able to haul more than 25 Blls and two logs on passing from Le Boeuf to Presqu'isle a few men have been employed in repairing that Road, all that they are able to perform is scarcely perceptible — French Creek still continuing but the Navigation of it has hitherto been but of little use on transportation, all these difficulties in the sending provision and forage from this place agrees to your opinion contained in your letter of the 19<sup>th</sup> ultimo

new York 14 Oct<sup>r</sup>. 1795

Sir

I was Yesterday afternoon honored with yours of the 10<sup>th</sup> Inst: enclosing a copy of your letter to mess<sup>rs</sup>. Lewis and Rawle, and of their opinion on the Points stated in it. — notwithstanding my Respect for the Talents and Candor of those Gentlemen, I do not hesitate to say, that the Cognizance and Powers given to the Commissioners designated in the 6 and 7<sup>th</sup> Articles of the Treaty are in my opinion vastly more comprehensive than those Gentlemen consider them — indeed I cannot conceive how it was possible to give the Commissioners greater Latitude, consistant with Reason & common sense, than by authorizing them to "decide the Claims in question according to the merits of the several Cases, and to Justice Equity and the Laws of Nations. — If it is asked what are the Claims and Cases which they are authorized to to decide? let it be answered in the Language of the Treaty, "all Claims for and cases of losses and Damages caused by irregular or illegal Captures or Condemnations of american Vessels or other Property, under colour of authority or Commissions from his Britannic majesty;" and in which cases Subject Compensation would not, for whatever Reason, be actually obtained had and received in the ordinary Courts of Justice —

The Duty of the Commissioners is two fold — first, to decide on the merits of all claims made in such cases, according to Justice Equity and the Laws of Nations, and Secondly, to ascertain and award the amount of the Losses & Damages sustained by those Claimants, in whose favor they decide the merits of the Case to be —

as on the one Hand no Legislature or Judicial acts in this country repugnant to the Treaty of Peace, can restrain the Commissioners under the 6<sup>th</sup> article from doing Justice to those Creditors — so on the other Hand, no royal Instructions or Decisions of Courts, given made or expressed contrary to the Laws of Nations, and causing Losses and Damages to american Citizens can restrain the Commissioners under the 7<sup>th</sup> article from doing that Justice to the Claimants, which Justice Equity and the Laws of Nations may prescribe — perfect Justice to all parties is the object of both the articles. if the Commissioners are empowered to do it in terms as explicit and comprehensive as the english Language affords —

I would with great pleasure take up and consider this subject at large and give you a formal Opinion upon it; but I must resist the Utility or Expediency, in the Present Moment, of bringing forward to the Merchants any other Description of hope— my opinions of mine relative to these or other articles of the Treaty —

after returning your letter I took the Liberty of communicating (this morning) to Col. Hamilton, the Opinions of M<sup>r</sup>. Lewis & M<sup>r</sup>. Rawle. — and I will his Hamilton enclose, open for your Inspection, a Letter from him to M<sup>r</sup> Woolcott, in which you will find his Sentiments on the Points in question —

I have the Honor to be &c —

51754:
Pittsburg 15<sup>th</sup> October 1795

Sir

When I was last at Fort Le Bœuf the Commanding Officer Ensign Joseph McCutcheon requested me to inform you that himself together with the Garrison under his command, Viz fifteen Men, are engaged under the Authority of the State of Pennsylvania and the Term for which his man are related expires on the last day of January next. But as it was expected that the whole of the State Troops would be balanced as soon as Gen<sup>l</sup> Sevier & M<sup>r</sup> Ellicott may have finished the Survey, for which they were appointed, which I believe is nearly completed. Neither the sixteen men at Le Bœuf nor any of the State Troops are furnished with winter Cloathing, therefore wishes either to be relieved by other Troops & disbanded or immediately to be furnished with suitable Cloathing for the ensuing Winter — The round Jackets & Trowsers on hand here Holloums would answer the purpose — for these sixteen men Blankets Shoes &Shirts are also wanted.

The Quarter Master General is reported here this day yet to have retiring from publick Service.

Col<sup>l</sup> Butler is yet at Fort Franklin — Expecting that new work encreases the expectations in the Q<sup>r</sup> Master Department of the upper posts an estimate of which will be transmitted by next post together with a general return of Stores here and an abstract of Instruments up to the first of the present Month.

You will please observe that there encloses herewith Cap<sup>t</sup> [undecipherable] Receipt for eleven hundred dollars appropriated for recruiting his Company at Presqu'isle.

I am Sir your very obedient
Humble Servant

Hend<sup>l</sup> Timothy Pickering

Sir,

Inclosed is an extract of a letter written to me by Brigadier Gen<sup>l</sup> Morrison with the copy of an Affidavit of Ben<sup>ja</sup> Kitchen — likewise the extract of a letter from B Gen<sup>l</sup> Seagrove to M Gen<sup>l</sup> Wayne inclosed to me by the last mentioned Officer.

I have thought it proper to forward this intelligence by Water as a Vessel is just sailing for Philadelphia & I understand the Gov is not at Augusta; which circumstance added to the delay of the Post might otherwise prevent this disagreeable information from reaching you for a considerable period — The frontier is in a state of Alarm & I fear many of the settlers will break — I have flattered the Midway settlement — one of the richest in this State and mentioned in Kitchen's affidavit with the prospect of support from the Artillery, as we understand that a peace has been concluded between the U States & the Northern Indians — It is highly unfortunate for our lower settlements that whether the fault lays with the Whites or Indians retaliation for losses by the latter is always made on them & what makes the case more hard is that the Indians are never injured or disturbed by those Settlers.

I have the honor to be &c

Savannah Oct<sup>r</sup> 16 1795

War Office Oct. 17. 1795.

Sir,

The President being about to return to this city, I wrote two letters, one to meet him at Baltimore, the other to go on to Mount Vernon, that receiving one or the other I might be favoured with his command on the subject of your request of leave of absence from the army, by post, in case bad roads should retard his arrival: but he has not arrived, nor have I received any letter, which I fully expected by this days post. I am sorry for this disappointment. The President will certainly be here the beginning of the ensuing week, & by next post you may expect his decision.

I am respectfully yours

T. Pickering

You will therefore please take the necessary Steps to have that Sum deducted from his Pay & inform me thereof. There appears to have been a Misunderstanding in the Relinquishment of that Part of Captain Greaton's Pay, it not having been considered for the use of his Family, and of Course was discontinued with you on the 1<sup>st</sup> of April 1794, owing perhaps to the Power of Attorney, not mentioning to be for the use of his Family. If therefore it should be the wish of Capt Greaton to continue the Relinquishment for the use of his Family, it will be necessary for him to procure your Certificate thereof and empower some Person to receive the amount; the power to set forth that the amount is for the use of his Family. If this will please inform me by the first Opportunity in expectation of hearing from you soon on the Subject of my last Letter.

I am

Sir &c

51788:
[Pickering, Timothy]

War Office October 19, 1795

Sir:

The deposition of Joseph Williams, Master of the Schooner Charlotte, of which the inclosed is a Copy, was sent to me by the British Chargé des Affaires at Philadelphia. The facts stated relative to the fitting out of the Privateer Ship Unicorn in the United States and that two of her Officers Peter Marshall and George Price, are American Citizens, I stated are already well known. These reasons and the outrage committed by them at Turks Island as well against a foreign nation as our own Ships and Citizens at that port require that particular vigilance be used to discover and seize that ship together with those and any other American Officers alike circumstanced, that they may be brought to justice, and the dignity of the laws and the good faith of the United States vindicated from the reproach to which they are exposed by the conduct of such unworthy Citizens. I therefore pray your Excellency to take such measures as are proper for the Executive of Georgia to accomplish the objects above mentioned. The additional evidence necessary for the conviction of the Offenders will doubtless be found on board the Unicorn or may otherwise be collected.

I have the honor to be

with great Respect

Your obedient Servant

[GA] Timothy Pickering

His Excellency
The Governor of Georgia

Sir,

I wrote you on the 20<sup>th</sup> instant. I acknowledged the receipt of your original and duplicate letter of the 13<sup>th</sup> of October, and informed you that M<sup>r</sup> Samuel Pifher had delivered to me two thousand, four hundred and fifty four dollars and forty one cents; for which sum I gave him my duplicate receit to be transmitted to the Accountant of the War Department for the due appreciation thereof. I delivered also to M<sup>r</sup> Pifher, one dollar and one cent, with a request that he would pay the same to you as the balance of my recruiting account, which from you will be pleased to pass on the receit to my credit.

You inform me that two thousand, seven hundred, and fifteen dollars, and seventy five cents have been passed to my credit from the receit rolls to the 30<sup>th</sup> of July last, which I have transmitted to you . . $2716.75

The amount of money paid on the receit rolls $3692.68
for the arrears of pay to the 30<sup>th</sup> June 1795

The amount of Philip Sandal debts . . . . 9.60
The amount of James Ruffley, Stilemore . . 36. —
[undecipherable] Samuel Taylor receit
Dollars $5739.75

From which I deduct
Henry [undecipherable] pay for July &c . —
John — his Bills . 4
Alexander Thompson . . 14. . 17.00

The amount, which, I supposed would [have] passed to my credit . . . $5722.75

There is a difference between your statement, and mine of five dollars.

The farther sum of forty eight dollars, which you also inform me has been passed to my credit, as paid to affinities, agrees with my Books.

In the pay roll, which I transmitted to you for the month of September, I placed Corporal James Robertson, who joined the company at West Point on the 25<sup>th</sup> of that month, as having due to him three months pay, making the sum of 18 dollars. Corporal William Garrison, who has pay due to him for the same term as the others of Captain Thompson's detachment, which joined on the 29<sup>th</sup> of August, was placed on the roll for the month of September only, and his pay due fifty dollars.

For the corrections of the pay roll, you sent me, I observe that five dollars are deducted from Robertson's pay, as made up in the roll from Governors Island, and 12 dollars from Garrison's is made up for July and August in a former pay roll. The two deductions making the amount of eighteen dollars.

Corporal Robertson, under a supposition that the whole amount of his pay is transferred to Governours Island, has sent to Lieutenant Taylor his receit for eighteen dollars; for if I have led him into a mistake, M<sup>r</sup> Taylor will of course refuse to pay him the money;

I shall in the mean time be attentive to your other corrections in the making out of the receit rolls for September, and shall trouble you to inform me again what sum was intended to be transmitted to me for the pay of Corporals Robertson and Garrison. The mistake has more than treble arisen at West Point, by the making a remark opposite to Garrison's name instead of Robertson, although in it not to be the copy of the muster and pay roll, which I have retained.

Three dollars have been stopped into the regimental chest, as the pay for July of Henry Fulford deceased, five dollars as the pay for the same month of Alexander Thompson, and four others as the pay of John Smith, both drummed out. I shall pay a particular attention to your directions on the money, which may henceforth remain in [strikethrough: the chest from] the deaths of the men, or from their being drummed out.

[Answer to Lieut Cox's letter.]

West Point, Oct<sup>r</sup> 26. 1798

Sir,

I owe justice to every Officer under my Command. Capt M. Kaltiesen, on hearing that you had laid charges against him, requested that a Court Martial should be assembled to investigate into his Conduct since his being Commissioner in the Corps of A & E. the Court of Enquiry delivered to me the charges, and according to the Articles of War, I required their opinion upon the Same; they have given their opinion, and it has been read by me upon the parade, as it was expressed by them. The Charges which you have to defend before the Court Martial, have no connexion with the charges laid by you before the Court of Enquiry; and I make no doubt but the Same justice which has been paid to Capt M. Kaltiesen, will also be paid to you. As my opinion will be Required upon the Sentence of the Court Martial which was not the case in the Court of Enquiry, I Refrain from answering the other part of your Letter.

I am Sorry to be under the Necessity of Refusing to you, to grant your Request to leave the Garrison

Signed L. Tousard

West Point, Nov. 10<sup>th</sup> 1795

Sir,

My last letter was dated the 22 Ultime, with which was enclosed two packets of vouchers & some other papers. I expected before now to have been able to have had my vouchers regularly arranged with certificates to them for the money I disbursed prior to M<sup>r</sup> Fisher's arrival here; but my great hurry of business has prevented my having them all completed. As many as I could get ready I now enclose you with an account of them. The remainder up to the time M<sup>r</sup> Fisher got here I will forward to you within a few days. I shall then with the greatest assiduity prepare the vouches I have for the money M<sup>r</sup> Fisher brought me, & forward them to you without delay. —

Your favors of the 30 & 31 Ultimo I have duly received. I have sent by a careful person going on his own business, my triplicate receipts to Col<sup>d</sup> Bush for the 267 dollars for the pay of the detachment of the legion under my direction. In a few days I shall receive said money. — I have for a few days been out of money, having paid out in a twice the money M<sup>r</sup> Fisher delivered me, and have been obliged to borrow 2<sup>15</sup> dollars since. — It gives me pain to have people call upon me for money when

when I have not any in my hands, to pay them agreeably to contract & under in compliance with Col<sup>d</sup> Benson's requisitions on me; which he informs me he is authorized to make for the accommodations of the regiment he belongs to. —

I have requested the hand the Secretary of War to forward to me for contingent expences at this garrison Three thousand dollars without the least delay. I suppose at this instant there are just demands upon me to this amount. — It is repugnant to my feelings to draw for a larger sum when so great a number of vouchers are in my hands not arranged yet properly to send; I will endeavor to make out with the sum I have now mentioned, until I forward more vouchers.

The artillerists & engineers' quarters are not yet all completed — and Col<sup>d</sup> Benson has not, and he says has not been able to spare any carpenters until the other day two or three only to repair the powder magazines & storehouses in which the military & quartermaster's stores are. I reported to the war department repeatedly from three in four years since a deplorable situation. The 8<sup>th</sup> one he will shortly be — have carpenters enough to repair them. More mechanics than have been employed on the artillerists & engineers' quarters, it

it was impossible to board & give lodgings to here.

I write this particularly to you on these subjects, not wishing to trouble Col<sup>d</sup> Pickering with a long letter, as his time must be entirely taken up with the very important business he has to transact in the two departments he is intrusted with the management of. — I am particularly attentive the Public receive full value for the money they out for them. —

I am, with the greatest esteem and respect, Sir, Your most obedient

Humble servant,

Geo: Fleming
[signature]

Will<sup>m</sup> Simmons Esquire.

[Indian Depredations
1795]

War-Office Nov. 12. 1795

Sir

On the 7th instant I received from General Jackson, M<sup>r</sup> Seagrove and Major Freeman, severally, dispatches communicating the afflicting news, of the murdering of seventeen Creek Indian men at or near Barrs Bluff on the Oconee. I do not hesitate to call this slaughter of those Indians murders; because if they had come to the settlements of the white people for the purpose of doing mischief, some evidence of their intention would appear by the mischief actually done: but of this neither of the letters give the least intimation. Besides, Timothy Barnards letter to M<sup>r</sup> Seagrove, forwarded to you by Gen<sup>l</sup>. Jackson, & by M<sup>r</sup> Seagrove to me, declares that of the five first who were killed, two (whom he names) were well known to M<sup>r</sup> Seagrove, to whom on a former occasion they had been sent as expresses, "and were as inoffensive men to the whites as any in the land, and the other three were as much so as they." Of Indians thus known to be friendly and well disposed, and whose persons and characters M<sup>r</sup> Barnard says were also well known to the people who killed them, no suspicion of their intending to do mischief could be warranted. These circumstances account for their coming into the settlement of the Whites

with that high confidence of safety which made them the unresisting victims of their atrocious murderers. Perhaps you will think I am too precipitate in pronouncing this opinion. Truly I shall be happy to find it a mistake, & to [strikethrough: tract] correct an erroneous judgement upon the facts. But this I do not expect. I wish it were as certain that the justice of the laws would operate effectually as that my opinion is well founded.

All the letters, Sir, with their inclosures were laid before the President, and I have it in command from him, to entreat your Excellency to use the utmost diligence & to exert all the powers with which you are invested, to bring the offenders to trial, and if guilty to punishment. This may possibly rescue from fatal retaliation many innocent inhabitants on your frontiers, or avert a still greater evil, a confirmed and general Indian war, from the Cumberland to the St. Marys. To hang a small band of assassins would be showing mercy to thousands of innocent citizens exposed to the vindictive resentments of the injured Indians. But I trespass on your Excellency by beginning

a detail of the destructive consequences of these murders, which may be immediately felt, and the more serious and extended mischiefs to be apprehended, if they pass with impunity: you must have anticipated them already.

With extreme solicitude to learn the result of your enquiries and exertions, I remain, with very great respect,

your Excellency's

most obedient Servant

Timothy Pickering

His Excellency George Matthews Esq<sup>r</sup>
Governor of the State of Georgia.

Sir

I have received your letter of the 7<sup>th</sup> inst.

On the [undecipherable: 4th?] 11 instant I sent forward to Presqu'isle forty beef cattle these when added to Provision previously sent forward will form a supply for the interior Garrison of Presqu'isle & Le Bœuf up to first of April 1796 except the Article of forage for the working Oxen was born — about that of which I am now endeavouring to send forward

I presume it will be necessary to have a proper boat or boats built at Presqu'isle for transportation of forage &ca from Cataraugus &Buffalos Creek from whence I have no doubt of a sufficient quantity being obtained at a reasonable rate. But it is an unfortunate Circumstance that the Saw Mills race & dam at that place was neglected until it became too late to complete it before the Winter as Hkasuns Plank &ca for the above purpose as well as for the Barracks might have been procured in one season.

Several of the Militia wagon horses were necessarily taken to carry the baggage &ca of of Parties on their march to Presqu'isle, and also frequently to carry the baggage of works of Provision Stores &ca by which several of them by excesses of fatigue &want of a full supply of forage have been so far reduced as not to be able to return. Others too have too, then have had their limbs broken in the almost impassable road from La Boeuf to Presqu'isle and these unavoidably perished — the proximity to these horses being employed on the above service has then appraised by competent Judges — as I was then apprehensive that some of them might be killed or fall

[No.] Philadelphia Nov. 17. 1798.

The interest you take in all public measures of importance, and the peculiar Solicitude you must feel at this time of general agitation, when so many are busy apparently to undermine the government which you so effectually labored to establish, and have so eminently contributed to maintain — induce me, with that Sincerity which I trust has ever marked my character, and that frankness which an entire confidence in your Judgement & candour inspires, to exhibit to your view the present Situation of the great public office.

Near three months have elapsed since the office of Secretary of State became vacant. At that moment matters of magnitude respecting the Treaty with Great Britain demanded attention, & the general business of the office could not be suspended. With the Presidents approbation I undertook the conducting of whatever required the uninterrupted agency of that office. Rging however to have been relieved long ere this time from the burthen. The President, I know, took immediate measures to fill the office. He first tendered it to Judge Patterson, then to Governor Johnson of Maryland, to General Pinckney &to Mr King, in Succession: and by all it has been refused. The three former nominations the President early communicated to me —

War-Office Nov. 24.1795.

Sir,

By the representation of Captain Kalteisen, I find the garrison at Fort Johnson is very ill accom-modated with quarters. The barracks are bad — there is no secure place for confining prisoners — nor any proper provision for keeping the ammunition necessary for the fort. Whether the fort should or should not be ceded to the United States, while there is a garrison of federal troops stationed there, I shall deem it my duty to provide for their being comfortably lodged; and the repairs and fastenings necessary for the preservation of the military stores and the safe keeping of prisoners must be made and provided. Captain Kalteisen will cheer-fully undertake to direct these small works; and I have a confidence that he will conduct the business properly and with economy. at any rate no engineer need be employed about them. I am so dissatisfied with M<sup>r</sup> Brault, that I think he must be discharged: on this however I shall write again. — The small sum indispensably necessary for the above mentioned re-pairs I beg you to Supply, on Capt. Kalteisen's order for paying for materials &workmen. I will with-out delay look into your expenditures, and put you in Cash, or reimburse what small sums you may advance.

I am very respectfully
Sir

War Office Nov. 26. 1795.

Sir,

Inclosed is a return of the ordnance & military stores laden on board the brigantine in which you will embark for S<sup>t</sup> Marys river. The nine pounders and one of the four pounders are to be placed in the fort near the town of S<sup>t</sup> Marys, with their proper ammunition and utensils. The two other four pounders with their ammunition, and a due proportion of the musket cartridges and accoutrements, tents, and one of the garrison flags, you will lodge at the post of Colerain, or where the post for the Indian trade shall be established.

A part of the troops embarking at the port of Philadelphia and at Richmond, destined for Saint Marys river being to take post at or near the town of S<sup>t</sup> Marys, you will give to the oldest officer there the charge of the ordnance & military stores proper to be left at that place: seeing that they are properly stored.

The counterpart for the brigantine in which you will embark, allows ten lay-days after your arrival at Colerain: for every day after the ten are elapsed the United States will be obliged to pay a demurrage of thirty dollars a day. Hence you will see the propriety of hastening the unloading of the brigantine.

Your military experience supercedes the necessity of suggesting the caution to be used in regard to the ammunition, not only for preserving it, but to guard against accidents from an explosion: it is hinted here merely because magazines proper or well fitted for its reception may be wanting; and which defect, if it exists, you will take the earliest measures to remedy, both at S<sup>t</sup> Marys & Colerain.

I am Sir your ob<sup>t</sup> Servant
Timothy Pickering
