52144:
To M<sup>r</sup> Edward Price.

It having been determined to establish a trading house on the River S<sup>t</sup>. Marys in the State of Georgia, for the purpose of supplying the Creek Indians with necessary Goods, provided agreeably to an act of Congress; you are hereby appointed the Factor for the purpose of conducting this Trade; in which the following instructions are to be observ'd.

The principle of the trade is to furnish the Indians with Goods at such moderate prices that the sales may simply reimburse to the United States the prime cost, and charges, [strikethrough: charges] you will find in the Invoices which will be delivered to you by the Surveyor.

2  The object of this trade is by supplying the Indians on such easy terms to manifest the liberality and friendship of the United States, and thus by the ties of Interest and gratitude to secure their attachments and lay the foundations of a lasting peace.

3  To provide against the numerous accidents and losses to which this trade will be liable, thirty three and a third per cent should be added to the Goods beyond the first cost, and charges. This is to be considered a general rule. You may find it necessary however to depart from it, by charging some articles lower, and some higher, in order [underline: the better] to satisfy the Indians in the course of the trade. But it will be important to fix early on the proper prices; and afterwards to adhere to them steadily. The Indians will then know what to depend on, and not to have their jealousy excited by the apprehension of unfair dealing, which a fluctuation of prices would be apt to beget.

4  The Goods are to be sold to the Indians either for Money or Peltries. For the Peltry the prices usually given by the Traders will naturally be your rule; and in this respect the habits of the Indians must govern. If these prices are so high that a loss would be incurr'd on the returns when brought to the Market in Philadelphia, such loss must be counteracted by an addition to the prices of [undecipherable]. A list of the sales at which Peltries are sold in Philadelphia

then will be furnished by the Surveyor. Instructions as to the manner to which your returns on Peltry are to be made as often as the quantity on hand and conveyances shall present; you will address them to the Surveyor.

5  James Seagrove Esq. the Superintendent of Indian Affairs in Georgia and his assistants (whose names and usual places of residence are subjoined) are to advertise the Indians of the establishment of this Factory, and of the benevolent principle on which it is to be conducted; and to invite them [strikethrough: the] to commence trading. On your arrival at St. Marys you will embrace the earliest opportunity to give notice thereof to the Superintendent, and of conveniency, to his Deputies. They will endeavour to furnish an Interpreter for the Factory.

6  One of the greatest difficulties to be apprehended is the demand of Goods on credit; either by the Indians themselves or the Indian Traders residing among them. But such credits are wholly inadmissible; and selling to the Traders with or without credit would be subversive of the main principle; for such traders would probably sell at their usual high prices; while the true object of the United States is to supply the Indians at moderate prices. And with these benevolent views of the United States you will on all occasions endeavour to make the Indians acquainted. If difficulties should occur in carrying on the trade, by the refusal of credit to the Indians, and by the total denial of goods to the Indian traders, you will make report thereof to the Department of War, stating facts with your opinion thereon and your ideas of the best mode of furnishing supplies to the Indians to effect the salutary objects indicated in these instructions.

7  The Surveyor will procure for you the necessary information as to the mode of saving and packing the Peltries, to ensure their getting to Market in good order.

8  M<sup>r</sup> Charles Anderson and Bustard are appointed to assist you in all the business of the Factory and you will take the earliest opportunities to make them acquainted with the business

to conduct it.

9  The commanding Officer of the Troops destined to serve on S<sup>t</sup>. Marys River will at all times furnish you with necessary Goods. One great object of their service is to protect this Indian trade.

10  Goods to the amount of One thousand five hundred Dollars are annually to be delivered to the Creek Station agreeably to treaty. That quantity you will now receive, and the same is to be separated from the Goods destined for trade, and delivered in the presence of M<sup>r</sup> Seagrove or of one of his Deputies pursuant to his orders.

11  M<sup>r</sup> Seagrove has recommended Colerain as the place most suitable for the establishment of the Factory; and this is to be accordingly attempted. He informs that some buildings erected there by him are well adapted to the object and may be occupied accordingly. Any repairs requisite to render them safe and tolerably convenient you will make. The commanding Officer of the Troops will probably be able to find among them the necessary mechanics to whom an allowance not exceeding one fifth of a dollar a day may be made for every reasonable day's work. You will furnish all the materials which must be purchased for repairing the Store house and any other buildings necessary for the accommodation of yourself, your Assistants and the Troops, to put them into comfortable quarters; of which a separate account is to be kept.

12  The hospital stores for the troops are to be in your custody, and issued on Returns signed by the Surgeon, expressing the names of the Sick for whom the stores are demanded.

13  You will keep a regular and frequent correspondence with the Surveyor, and in cases which appear to you proper, with the Department of War, to which all your dispatches for the Surveyor may be directed.

14  You and your Assistants and others necessary to be employed, are all to be dieted at the public expense; but you will keep an exact account thereof as well of what shall be drawn from the Stores as of what you shall purchase; and in both it is expected that the most œconomy will be observed.

15  If the trade should succeed, the Store may of course be exhausted of some particular kinds of Goods. You will from time to time give the earliest notice thereof making your remittances which must be [strikethrough: the] the source for [strikethrough: other] supplies.

16  It would have been extremely desirable to carry on this trade with the Indians, without the use of Rum; but from an apprehension that the habits of Indians in this respect could not be controlled that article has been provided. Still however you are to use your endeavours by friendly advice to the Indians to persuade [strikethrough: them] them to let it alone; taking care not to hazard their disgust. But if you find that Rum must be sold to them, let it be in such small quantities as may guard them against drunkenness during their continuance at the Post; for which you will give them this reason — That while trading you desire them to remain sober that they may know what they do, and be satisfied that the trade is perfectly fair and honest. When they are ready to depart, such quantities as they desire to carry with them and the Stock will allow for balances due them, may be delivered.

17  The forms of the accounts and returns you are to render will be furnished by the Comptroller of the Treasury; but in default of their timely arrival, your knowledge of accounts will enable you to form a mode that cannot fail of being satisfactory untill you can receive them.

18  I close these instructions with suggesting to you the necessity of kind and friendly treatment of the Indians who may visit your Station and of perfect candour in all your dealings with them. Patience in particular will be requisite and caution when any of them get drunk. To avoid the latter evil you will use your endeavours with the influential men among them to draw them off from the Station as soon as their traffick is over; and untill then you may continue as above suggested to make but small issues of rum.

Given at the War-Office of the United States the 26<sup>th</sup> of November 1796.

Timothy Pickering.

52186:
Philadelphia, 30 Nov<sup>r</sup> 1795

Sir

As the late Transactions at Rhode Island, which involved two of His Majestys Officers, in the Censure of this Government, have been long since submitted to the Issue of a Discussion between His Majestys Ministers and the Ministry of the United States, in London, I shall, in the Communication I am now about to make to you, avoid, as much as possible, any recurrence to the Subject, other than what relates to the contemplated Demands, contained in your letter to me of the 5 of last: After requiring Capt Home for the Causes therein Assigned, to Remove from his Station, within the Jurisdiction of the United States, in a limited Time, another Demand was to follow which was to extend to the liberation of three Seamen, "whom within that Jurisdiction" Capt Home was said, to have "unlawfully seized."

In my Letter to you of the 8 of Sept I readily admitted that the Detention of any Vessel within the Territorial Jurisdiction of the United States, and the Arrest of any part of her Crew, in that position, could not be justified; but being then totally uninformed as to the Facts, independently of the Express Protest of Capt Tillinghast and others, which you were pleased to inclose to me,

I took immediate measures, as well for the satisfaction of this Government, as to wipe away any Imputation against a man of high Rank in his Majestys Service, to enquire, into the truth of these Allegations; It turned out as I expected, it would, that Capt Home had failed, before my Inquiries reached him; a Circumstance, which accounts for the Delay that has happened in procuring the necessary Explanations.

From the Information now in my possession, I am authorized to say, that at this Time Capt Briefs Packet and the Ann, Capt Tillinghast, were respectively brought to by his Majestys Ship Africa; neither of these Vessels was within the Territorial Jurisdiction of the United States. Having pointed my Inquiries to meet the expectation of this Government relative to the Seamen impressed from on Board the Ship Ann, I avoid, for the Reason I have above Assigned, any further Observation relative to the Rhode Island Packet.

The original Paper signed, William Jones, &c and George White, a Copy of which I have now the Honor to inclose to you, was received by me this Day under Cover of Capt Home — It serves to Refute two Facts, which seem in some Degree, to have accelerated the marked Resentment

of this Government against that Officer — It proves, by the Acknowledgment of the parties supposed to be injured, that these three Seamen were not "unlawfully seized, within the Jurisdiction of the United States. And that to these Seamen, in point of Citizenship, this Country has no Claim upon any Principles which His Majestys Government has Recognized; on the Contrary it unequivocally ascertains, that they were, natural born Subjects of the Crown. Moreover, it tends to establish, among innumerable glaring proofs an unceasing Exertion of Craft and Intrigue, calculated to unhinge that Harmony between the two Countries, which it is the earnest wish of our respective Governments, to cultivate and main-tain — I have the Honor to be with due Consideration & Respect,

Sir,      Your most Obed<sup>t</sup>
H<sup>ble</sup> Serv<sup>t</sup> —

A Statement of the progress in providing materials for the Frigates and in building them.

If the Frigates had been constructed with the timber at hand, in the several places where they were destined to be built, they might by this time have been completed. But the design of rendering them permanently useful, having determined the Executive to have them constructed with live Oak and Cedar, the measures deemed necessary and adequate to the procuring of those materials were taken during the last year. The common and easy acquisition of these articles in the ordinary service of the merchants forbade any apprehension of extraordinary difficulty in procuring the same for the frigates. But in the experiment it has been found that timber of the lengths and sizes necessary for frigates was greatly dispersed and grew generally in places difficult of access and required extraordinary means of transportation to the landing. The natural difficulties of the country have been increased by unusual quantities of rain. Ship carpenters were sent from the Northern States to the colonies having the live Oak, and employed during the last winter in cutting and hewing the timber; but the climate deterred them from staying to prosecute their work, so that those men only capable of selecting the proper timber and moulding it in the requisite forms have been prevailed on to remain. "A TREATY OF PEACE, between the United States of America and the tribes of Indians called the Wyandots, Delawares, Shawanoes, Ottawas, Chippewas, Putawatimes, Miamis, Eel-rivers, Weea Kickapoos, Piankashaw and Kaskaskias.

To put an end to an diffusive war, to settle all controversies and to restore harmony and a friendly intercourse between the said United States and Indian tribes ; Anthony Wayne, major-general, commanding the army of the United States, and sole commissioner for the good purpose above-mentioned, and the said tribes of Indians, by their sachems, chiefs and warriors, met together at Greeneville, the head quarters of the said army, have agreed on the following articles, which, when ratified by the President, with the advice and consent of the Senate of the United States, shall be binding on them and the said Indian tribes.

ARTICLE 1<sup>st</sup>. Henceforth all hostilities shall cease; peace is hereby established, and shall be perpetual; and a friendly intercourse shall take place, between the said United States and Indian tribes.

ARTICLE 2<sup>d</sup>. All prisoners shall on both fides be restored. The Indians prisoners of the United States Shall be immediately set at liberty. The chiefs of the United States Still remaining prisoners among the Indians, Shall be delivered up in ninety days from this date, being to the general commanding officer at Greeneville, Fort Wayne, or Fort Defiance; and ten chiefs of the said tribes shall remain at Greeneville as hoftages, untill the delivery of the prisoners shall be effected.

ARTICLE 3<sup>d</sup>. The general boundary line between the lands of the United States, and the lands of the said Indian tribes, Shall begin at the mouth of Cayahoga river, and run thence up the fame to the portage between that and the Tuscaraways branch of the Muskingum; thence down that branch to the crossing place above Fort Lawrence; thence wefterly to a fork of that branch of the great Miami river running into the Ohio, or patawa, which is called Loromie's Store, and where commences the portage between the Miami of the Ohio, and St. Mary's river, which is a branch of the Miami, which runs into

Baltimore 9<sup>th</sup> July 1796

Dear Sir, I last post brought me a letter, but of a trouble nature I suppose the brigade business, has been discussed in “says” and brought to a Conclusion — I Shall be glad to hear as soon as possible, what that Conclusion is — I Suppose you have Seen an extract from the very long Journal of the St Hasard, with its Damn nasional conclusions, blaming the raising of the frigates here — When I look up the paper I am mist & I Suspected it that Some of Stoddert's Nonsense had immediately Sent to the other printers, and desired my Souls not to print the pieces but on Asking Stoddert if he was the Author of it, to wit — a question that he was not, Nor did he know who was — I must Confess I have been very much Ashamed, at Seeing the pieces, least they never might Suppose, it was published by Some one Concerning our hurting the brigade — Should any one mention to you that they he go rather, my olden or any of the Navy Officers to be the Author of these rediculous pieces, you will please to deny it — I am your very Obt

NB the accounts I have Seen in the other Thomas Truxtun paper, respecting the raising of the Frigates, is Modest and true, then flattering to Stoddert but the Maryland Journal is too much in the Jacobine Stile.

Department of State Jan<sup>y</sup> 7. 1796.

Sir,

On the first instant, according to a previous arrangement, the Minister of the French Republic presented to the President of the United States the colours of France. This was on Friday, and Congress did not meet again till the following Monday, when the colours were presented to the two Houses of Congress with a message from the President and the papers mentioned in it, to wit, an address from the committee of public safety dated the 21<sup>st</sup> of October 1794, the speech of the French Minister on presenting the colours to the President, and the President's answer, of all which copies are inclosed.

After the exhibition in the House of Representatives, the House passed unanimously the inclosed resolve; in pursuance of which to make known their sentiments to the Representatives of the French people, the President has addressed a letter to the Directory of the French Republic, which you will find inclosed, and which you will take the earliest opportunity to deliver.

With the resolve of the House of Representatives, the President has thought fit to communicate to the Directory, the resolve of the Senate on the same subject, altho' not officially desired to do it. — Thus there will be seen a concurrence of all the branches of the Government representing the people of the United States in the same affection & friendship for the French Republic. — Copies of that letter & of these resolves for your own information, you will find also inclosed.

In your letter of the 20<sup>th</sup> of October (the last which has been received) you say that as yet no complaints had been made against our treaty with Great Britain, nor had you heard any thing from the committee on the subject, since their application relative to certain reports respecting it — yet in your postscript you express your opinion that if ratified it would excite great discontents.

On this point I can only again refer you to my letter of the 25<sup>th</sup> of September, in which it is demonstrated, that in a pointing to the terms of that treaty, the United States infringe no stipulation & violate no duty towards France. And you have seen by M<sup>r</sup>. Randolph's communications last Summer, that all the objections started by the French Minister were completely removed.

The treaty of peace made by General Wayne with the Indian tribes northwest of the river Ohio has been ratified by the President with the unanimous advice & consent of the Senate. The Cherokees and Creeks are also at peace with us. Such perfect tranquillity on all our borders was never known since we became an Independent People. But in the midst of the universal joy which this state of things excited, a few ruffians in Georgia committed some atrocious murders on about twenty Creeks. This was in September. Severe retaliation is to be feared; the endeavours were immediately used to ward off the evil. As yet I have heard of but one family that has been struck —

I have the honor to be with great respect
Sir,
Your Obedient Servant.
Timothy Pickering.

52590:
West Point, January 15<sup>th</sup> 1796

Sir,

I have received your letter of the 6th instant. Colonel Rochefontaine arrived here on the 9th of the month, and paid into my hands Two Thousand, Six Hundred and Nineteen Dollars and Eighty Cents, for which sum you will receive by this post my duplicate receipt.

I enclose to you the muster and pay roll for the month of December, 1795 of the Corps of Artillerists and Engineers at this garrison. Such of the officers at West Point, among whom I place myself, as have not drawn their rations from the contractor, request that the money for their Subsistance might be remitted to them through the same channel as their monthly pay. I have consequently inclosed for your inspection Statements of the respective amounts due, accompanied by certificates; references to which Statements are made on the pay roll.

A court martial, held at West Point on the 2<sup>d</sup> of December 1795, has ordered that Stoppages to refund certain expences, Should be made from the pay of

Henry Starks private in the 3<sup>d</sup> Company 3 Battal.
James Welles private } mustered on 8<sup>ber</sup> from the
Theoph.<sup>s</sup> McBride private } W<sup>t</sup> to the 2<sup>d</sup> Com.<sup>y</sup> 4<sup>th</sup> Batt.<sup>l</sup>

I transmit you an extract from the Sentence, and would request you to send me a memorandum of the ordnance prices of the different Articles of arms, accoutrements and uniform clothing, that I may know when to place the men again on the pay roll. Henry Starks has been detained on no pay roll from West Point, nor can I ascertain from him or otherwise the day on which he was apprehended. James Welles was placed on the pay roll for November last. Theophilus McBride was paid to the 30th of June, 1795, was a deserter four days; and is included also in the pay roll for November last. The eight Dollars which are in my hands for the pay of the two latter, for November, I shall State in my accounts as forfeited to the United States. You will be pleased to inform me, if the pay due in arrears to the first and last of these men when they deserted, be considered as part of the Stoppages ordered to be made. Henry Starks was taken in the neighbourhood of Springfield by Captain Cotton of the Legion.

Warrant James Henneck has represented to me that, when he was under the command of Captain Gamble, he enlisted Thomas Bunyan and paid him ten dollars on account of his bounty; that the receipt was never returned in any of Capt. Gamble's accounts, and that both the sum paid by himself, and the four dollars balance of bounty coming to Thomas Bunyan, are fall due by the United States. I enclose for your inspection Bunyan's inlistment, his receipt for the ten dollars paid him by Serjeant Henneck, and Serjeant Henneck's account for the same. Thomas Bunyan is mustered in the 2<sup>d</sup> company 4th Battalion.

Colonel Rochefontaine has delivered to me fifty four blank receit rolls, for which I thank you.

I transmit you also a muster and pay roll of a Detatchment, which has joined in December, from Captain Blackburn; and to which, it has been stated to me, arrearages of pay are due.

I have the honour
to be with respect,
Sir,

Your very humble Servant
Nath. Freeman Lieut. A&E
Temp. Paymaster at West Point

[William Simmors Esquire]

Dear Sir,                                        Jany 21. 1796.

I inclose a letter from Capt. Blackburn, which I request you to peruse, with the letter from Gen<sup>l</sup> Knox, & the certificate on oath of Jesse Taylor, relative to 150 dollars paid to the late lieutenant Grayson, who spent the money without getting recruits. The simple question, in my opinion, is this — Whether [strikethrough: or] Capt. Blackburn was justifiable in putting that sum into Grayson's hand who had just been commissioned in the same corps of artillery, and instructed by the Secretary of War to assist Capt. Blackburn in recruiting? — I will observe, that subalterns are every day employed to enlist recruits, and are furnished with money for the purpose. And I have no hesitation in expressing my opinion, that Capt. Blackburn was justifiable in the payment of that sum for that purpose to lieut. Grayson — who is since dead, & left no property. He was the son of the late Col<sup>o</sup>. Grayson. — Lieut. Grayson's rect. has been left — which has occasioned the production of W<sup>m</sup>. Taylor's certificate. — Capt. Blackburn has met with such a reception from the Accountant, on this business, that he talked of resigning. I advised him to the contrary, & to obtain evidence of the advance

advances to Grayson, when I could not doubt the admission of it to his credit.

The fact seems to be that the Accountant sets down every man entrusted with public money for a rascal — & treats him accordingly, when he comes to settle his accounts.

I shall be obliged by your opinion before I give any order in this case.

Y<sup>rs</sup> Sincerely
T. Pickering

M<sup>r</sup> Wolcott

West Point, January 2<sup>d</sup> 1796.

Sir,

A demand was lately made upon the regimental chest at West Point for the advancement of fifteen dollars to purchase amputating and other chirurgical instruments. A question arose in the council of administration on the propriety of affording the sum required from the chest. The Commandant of the Corps offered, that the money remaining in my hands as due to deputies, being public property could be appropriated to public uses; that the council of administration had the power, not indeed of settling pecuniary accounts, but of inspecting into their nature, and ordering such advance of money upon them, as exigencies might demand; and that their accounts, being afterwards Subject to your examination, would obtain their final Settlement at your office. The surplus of deputies, in which money would be immediately wanted, was offered as a proof, that the Council of Administration ought to have some controul over the money in the chest, not doubly appropriated.

On the other hand it was urged, that no money had, as yet, been remitted to West Point for the contingent expences of the corps; that the Temporary Paymaster had alone Signed the recits for that, which had hitherto been Sent for the pay and forage of the regiment;

my account were alone responsible for its expenditure; that the money was appropriated by you to particular purposes; and that the accidental balance, which remained, by the deputies of felding in his hands, belonged to the Treasury of the United States, and could not, either by the Council of Administration, or the Temporary Paymaster, be Sent away without the previous knowledge or advice of the proper, from whom it had been received; and that you, being the officer appointed by law for the Settlement of unliquidated military accounts had directed that Similar demands Should be transmitted to your office, and that you could inform the Temporary Paymaster of this affair. Captain Troup and the Temporary Paymaster agreed in this opinion.

I would be extremely Sorry, if I found by misconception, objects in the Smallest degree, the views of the Commandant, actuated alone by zeal for the Service, and well regulated policy of the Corps. I acknowledge my situation to be novel, and therefore place less dependence on my opinion, than if it had been ripened by mature judgement, or Sanctioned by long experience. Acting as Paymaster I conceive myself to be under your direction.

If therefore my conduct has been reprehensible, a few lines from you will Set it right. As I have been governed by what I thought my duty, I Shall not be ashamed to confess, on conviction, my error, and promise to do better.

I have the honour to be

with respect,
Sir,

Your very humble Servant,

W<sup>m</sup>. Freeman Lieut. A<sup>t</sup>C.
Temp<sup>s</sup>. Paymaster at West Point

William Simmons Esquire

century I have observed with great Satisfaction that the utmost accuracy has been observed by you in all your transactions as Paymaster. If at any time you should be at a loss for any Information which I can give — I shall do it with pleasure.

I have to observe in reply to your letter of the 2<sup>d</sup> Instant enclosing the directions of the Commanding Officer for placing on the Pay Roll sundry men who have not received their additional Bounty, that this mode I do not approve of. If the Officer who Inlisted the men will Settle his Recruiting Account there will be no difficulty, the money shall be immediately furnished. This shows the necessity of all Accounting Officers Settling their account without delay, and I have to request that you will represent that there are a number of Officers who have not yet Settled their accounts and that I am determined to Stop their Pay, unless they Shall furnish them together with the Vouchers — Besides these are some Officers who have received sums of Money a long time since for the Pay of their men, and they never have yet furnished the Receipts, tho' I have repeatedly required them to do it. Sir

I received your letter of the 23<sup>d</sup>. ultimo — respecting the receipt I transmitted to you.

I dont know what you wish to allude to in mentioning officers paid in three different capacities, it cannot be alluding to Mess<sup>rs</sup> Foreman and McAlabn, for I dont wish to recommend them for other extrapay than that of Adjutant, one of the Second and the other of the third Battalion, both allowed by the laws of organisation.

I wish to establish some kind of regulations respecting the corps which is entrusted to my care, and which is the wildest reunion of men that ever existed, without any check to their bad inclinations, the strongest mean is the Stoppages on their pay for cleanliness and keeping their cloaths in good repair; M<sup>r</sup> Freeman observed that you had given him orders to pay very month, to every Soldier, and to let this Soldier do of his money what he pleased.

I received Demands of many men respecting the 6 Dollars that are to be paid on their Joining the corps, I referred them to M<sup>r</sup> Freeman, who informed me that application had been made to you, and that you had not granted those demands, because the officer who had recruited them had not fulfilled their accounts for recruiting with you. as the law has not contemplated that circumstance of neglect in the officer recruiting, is it possible to avoid the fulfillment of the promise under that consideration? if the law is to be executed at all events, even at the risk of the U. S. losing Money for misplaced confidence, I wish you would enable me to Stop Such claims in the corps.

in two or three circumstances, M<sup>r</sup> Freeman has told me that he was the only one accountable for the money paid to the corps, & that he might in consequence of his orders from you, dispense with lodging money transmitted to him in the Military Chest, which is under the direction of the council of Administration, as that Idea is [strikethrough: Erroneous] I did not dwell upon it, and I concluded that he misunderstood you, for how could it be that an officer whom I appoint, and whom I may destitute of his office of Pay Master, might receive orders unknown to me, and act contrary to the regulations pointed out by a Special decision of the Secretary of war, which I have the honor to transmit to you for your general

by it you will see that the council of Administration has the charge of the Monies transmitted to the corps, and that it is to be lodged in the Chest & those keys; that the Pay Master is no more responsible than the two other members, and that the Pay Master is only responsible for what Sums are intrusted to him from time to time for the pay or any other expenses. I have no doubt but you will think preferable in future, to direct the Sums to be paid to the Council of Administration than to the Pay M<sup>r</sup> who may not be a M<sup>r</sup> Freeman, well informed & as regular in every thing he transacts as M<sup>r</sup> Freeman — it would remove also that difficulty which feels disagreeable to him, that of giving before hand his own receipt for money which is to be received at New York by another; if he was an imprudent young man, as I have Seen many, and as it might be the case if M<sup>r</sup> Freeman was to resign his commission, he might chuse for receiving the Public money, another location, and this law would show that a council composed of the [undecipherable: commanding] or the commissioned officers of the corps, and the Junior Captain added to the young man Pay Master, would generally make a better choice. — you will

consider the advantages and inconveniences, and you will propose me your wishes on that Subject. but you will receive the letter I transmit to you, the copy of which you will find in the Books of the war office.

please to Send me the return of the prices allowed to the contractors for every kind of Cloathing for the army, in order that I Should regulate the Stoppages for clothing delivered them above this allowance.

Sir

The Secretary of the Treasury has shown me an Account in which there is a large sum charged for relivering Copper bolts. If this work is still going on, pray let it be immediately stopped. February 6<sup>th</sup> 1796

Sir

Your favours of the 7<sup>th</sup> and 25<sup>th</sup> November last was received at the time that the Legislature of this State was in Session, and was Submitted to their consideration. The Assembly in consequence passed an act of which the enclosed is a copy. and in conformity to that Act I have now the honour to transmit to you the copies of twenty five sets of pay Bills duly Authenticated, for Militia Services performed at the expence of the United States at certain periods when the Assistance & powers was rendered in me by the President of the United States to employ them at the instance of the Numbers, to the end that the same may be adjusted, and the amount which accrues to this State by the several Governments.

They are stated in the manner directed by the Laws of this Commonwealth and approved of in me agreeable thereto, In some instances where the militia were called out on sudden emergencies, they were obliged to furnish their own rations, and in other cases where the rations were so small as not to make it an offence with any one to supply them for the price

allowed by law they also furnished themselves with provisions in those instances the amount of rations are carried out on the pay rolls in Separate colum at eight cents p<sup>r</sup> ration, the price allowed and paid by this Government. In other cases the rations was furnished by persons contracted to do so, and copies of the Abstracts for the same now accompany the pay Rolls.

I have empowered Christopher Greenup and Alexander D. Orr [undecipherable] now representing this State of Kentucky in the Congress of the United States to act as agents or Attorneys in fact in behalf of this State, for the purposes [strikethrough: specified] authorized by the act referred to, to the department of those Accounts and to receive the amount in money and to pay the same into the treasury of the Commonwealth.

Many of these pay Rolls are but of small amount and I flatter myself the President will conceive that those expences are very inconsiderable when compared with the magnitude of the objects to which they have been directed.

The short time that these detachments of Militia have been continued on duty affords a sufficient ground for a belief that they were dismissed the moment that their service was not indispensably necessary and I trust will induce the President of the United States to direct that the same may be reimbursed without

without delay, to this State.

The three Garrisons posted on the Wilderness Road were all discharged on the eighth day of January last, under the impression that their services was not necessary at this time, a firm and general peace with all the Indian tribes.

I have the Honour to be with very great respect and Esteem

Sir
Your Most Ob<sup>t</sup> servant
Isaac Shelby

The Hon<sup>ble</sup>
Timothy Pickering
Secretary of War

[Copy]

West Point, February 11<sup>th</sup> 1796

Sir,

The honour of your letter of yesterday's date has been received. The papers, which accompanied it will be transmitted with the next muster roll to the Accountant to the War Department; and the Statements of bounty, to which you refer, will be made at the same time. The monthly muster and pay roll for January will be submitted to the Commanding Officers inspection and signature with the same punctuality as the others have been. By the observation made to you some time past, on the companies' monthly muster rolls, I meant no more than to obtain your advice. It had been directed by a former Commanding Officer, that they should be lodged with the Paymaster. You have given different orders, and they shall be obeyed.

The directions, which I have received from the Accountant to the War Department on the subject of the money in my hands, and which I have communicated to you, must account for my past conduct.

Your letter of yesterday's date surprised me because it was unexpected, but although from deference to your advice, I delayed an immediate answer, an honest heart and a well intentioned mind pointed out a ready reply.

[signature]

Philadelphia Feb<sup>y</sup> 15th 179c

Sir

Agreeably to your request I have paid the strictest attention to the contents of Mr. Joshua Humphreys letter to you of the 13th inst. and after mature deliberation cannot coincide with his opinion of putting the cedar toptimbers into the ships in two pieces instead of one entire piece. I have always considered the timbers composing the frames of both classes of frigates already too small (that is) they are sided 2 inches less than what was absolutely requisite according to my opinion for ships of such magnitude and capacity. It has been generally supposed that the principal strength of a Vessel when at sea depends on her carrying a press of (torn off) & also that during a calm, or heavy sea running she rolls without straining, which cannot be the case if her timbers are narrow, for on the breadth of the surfaces of her timbers against her plank, as well as the plank laying close to the timbers will lye a great part of her strength, as the larger her timbers are sided the greater will be the distance between the fenner and other fastening of her body on which lies the principal strain.
